title: Data Protection, Records, and Information Systems

content.text: This section sets out policies and procedures to protect personal data, manage school records and govern information systems. It has three purposes:

items: Protect privacy rights: Make sure personal data is collected, processed, stored and disposed of in line with legal requirements and ethical standards. This covers students, staff, parents and other stakeholders.
Maintain record integrity: Set up systematic record-keeping that supports educational excellence, regulatory compliance and organizational accountability.
Ensure system security: Use technical and organizational measures to protect information systems against unauthorized access, data breaches and operational disruptions.
content.title: 14.1.1 Purpose

content.text: Good data protection and records management are essential. They keep stakeholder trust, meet accreditation standards and fulfill legal obligations under Indonesian law and Cambridge requirements.
This section applies to all data and information systems the school uses, including but not limited to: Academic Systems:

items: EduNav School Information System (SIS): Student enrollment, attendance, grades, behavior tracking, parent communication
Cambridge examination systems: CIE Direct, Admin Hub, Results Plus
EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation) assessment platform
Learning Management Systems and digital learning platforms
content.title: 14.1.2 Scope of Application

items: Dapodik (Data Pokok Pendidikan): Indonesian Ministry of Education data reporting system
SIMPKB (Sistem Informasi Manajemen Pengembangan Keprofesian Berkelanjutan): Teacher professional development tracking
Financial management systems: Accounting software, payroll systems
Human Resources systems: Staff files, recruitment databases
Facility management systems: Asset registers, maintenance logs
School email accounts and institutional communication platforms
Parent communication applications
Website and social media accounts
CCTV and security monitoring systems

content.text: The school processes several types of data. Each type has its own protection requirements: Student Personal Data:

items: Biographical information: Full name, date of birth, gender, nationality, address, contact details
Family information: Parent/guardian names, contact details, family structure
Academic records: Enrollment history, grade transcripts, assessment results, attendance records, disciplinary records
Special category data: Medical/health information, photographs and videos, behavioral support records, safeguarding/child protection records
Cambridge examination data: Candidate numbers, exam entries, results, access arrangements
content.title: 14.1.3 Data Categories

items: Employment records: Job applications, employment contracts, references, professional qualifications
Performance data: Appraisal records, professional development history, lesson observations
Financial information: Payroll details, tax information, bank account numbers
Special category data: Criminal background checks (safeguarding), medical information (occupational health), immigration documents (KITAS/KITAP for expatriate staff)
Contact information: Names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses
Communication records: Meeting notes, correspondence, complaint records
Consent records: Permissions for trips, photo/video use, medical treatment
Financial records: Budgets, invoices, receipts, procurement records, donor information (if applicable)
Vendor information: Supplier contracts, service provider details
Facility and asset data: Inventory lists, maintenance records, security logs

content.text: Several regulatory frameworks govern the school's data protection practices: Indonesian Legal Requirements:

items: UU No. 27/2022 tentang Pelindungan Data Pribadi (Personal Data Protection Law): This law sets out the rights of data subjects. It also sets out the obligations of data controllers/processors and the penalties for non-compliance. Implementing regulations are still being developed. Schools must monitor and adapt to new requirements.
Ministry of Education regulations: Dapodik data reporting requirements, SIMPKB integration, student records retention under national education standards
Indonesian Archives Law: Requirements for retention and disposal of official records
Employment law: Staff data protection obligations under labor regulations
Tax regulations: Financial records retention for audit purposes
content.title: 14.1.4 Legal and Regulatory Framework

items: Cambridge Assessment International Education requirements: Data protection obligations under UK GDPR (Cambridge operates from UK); secure handling of examination data; candidate confidentiality
CIS (Council of International Schools) Standards: Domain G (Premises, facilities, technology systems and auxiliary services) - emphasis on secure data systems and ethical information governance

WASC (Western Association of Schools and Colleges) Accreditation: Category A (Organization) - Evidence-based governance and record-keeping; Category D (Resources) - Technology infrastructure and data security
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) principles: GDPR does not apply directly to Indonesian schools. It still provides an international best practice framework that aligns with UU PDP
ISO/IEC 27001: Information security management standards
Educational Records Bureau (ERB) guidelines for international schools

content.text: Clear data protection responsibilities make each person accountable and help the school carry out the policy: Principal (Data Controller):

items: Final responsibility for data protection compliance and for carrying out the policy
Approves Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)
Makes decisions on high-risk data processing activities
Works with the Board/Foundation on data protection governance
Makes the final decision on data subject requests (access, correction, erasure)
Accountable for data breach response and notification
content.title: 14.1.5 Roles and Responsibilities

items: Carries out the technical data security measures
Manages system access control (user accounts, permissions, audit logs)
Backup and disaster recovery procedures
Data quality assurance for Dapodik/SIMPKB reporting
First responder to data security incidents
Trains staff on technical data protection measures
Manages vendors that process data for the school (third-party data processors)

A Data Protection Officer is mandatory if any one of the three tests in UU No. 27/2022 Article 53 is met. The first test is processing for public services. The second is a core activity that needs large-scale, regular and systematic monitoring. The third is a core activity that involves large-scale processing of specific or criminal personal data. Schools process children's health and safeguarding data at scale. They should assess themselves against these tests, not against headcount
Monitoring compliance with data protection policy and regulations
Providing advice on DPIAs and complex data protection issues
Acting as contact point for data subjects and regulatory authorities
Conducting internal data protection audits
Note: Smaller schools may give DPO responsibilities to the Principal or IT Manager as an extra duty
Student data accuracy and completeness in EduNav
Coordination between academic records and Dapodik reporting
Management of Cambridge candidate data
Student records retention and archiving
Staff personal data management
Employment records retention and secure disposal
Coordination with IT Manager on staff system access
Background check records security (safeguarding files)
Cambridge examination data security
Secure credentials management for Cambridge systems
Candidate confidentiality during results processing
Liaison with Cambridge on data-related incidents
Secure management of child protection records
Extended retention schedule for safeguarding files (see Section 8)
Access control for highly sensitive safeguarding data
Following the data protection policy in daily work
Secure handling of student and staff information
Immediate reporting of data security concerns or breaches
Completion of mandatory data protection training
Following the clean desk policy and secure disposal procedures

content.text: Data protection is a core part of the school's overall quality management and accreditation readiness:

items: EduNav Platform: Central store for student and staff data; real-time dashboards for leaders to monitor; evidence collection for the accreditation self-study

content.text: The school follows internationally recognized data protection principles. They are in line with UU No. 27/2022 (Indonesian Personal Data Protection Law) and GDPR best practices: Principle 1: Lawfulness, Fairness, and Transparency

items: Lawfulness: All data processing has a valid legal basis. UU No. 27/2022 Articles 20-21 set out six bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public interest and legitimate interest
Fairness: Data is used in ways that data subjects would reasonably expect. There is no hidden or deceptive processing
Transparency: Clear, easy-to-read privacy notices tell data subjects how their data is used. The notices are in both English and Bahasa Indonesia
content.title: 14.2.1 Data Protection Principles

items: Data is collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes
Without new consent, data is not used for purposes that are incompatible with the original purpose
Example: Student photos taken for yearbook cannot be used for commercial marketing without separate consent
The school collects only data that is adequate, relevant and necessary for the purpose
Admissions forms do not ask for unnecessary information (e.g., parents' salary details, unless required for a financial aid assessment)
Data collection forms are reviewed regularly to remove fields that are no longer used
The school takes reasonable steps to keep data accurate and up to date
Annual data check: Parents review and update student information at the start of each academic year
Staff are responsible for telling HR about changes to their personal details (address, emergency contacts, qualifications)
Correction procedures for inaccurate data (see Section 14.2.3)
Data is kept only as long as necessary for the purpose, or as required by law
Full records retention schedule (see Section 14.5)
Secure disposal procedures when the retention period ends
Exception: Student academic transcripts are kept permanently (lifetime educational record)
Appropriate technical and organizational measures protect data against unauthorized access, loss, or destruction
Physical security: Locked filing cabinets, restricted access areas
Digital security: Password protection, encryption, access controls, regular backups
Staff training on secure data handling practices
The school is responsible for showing that it complies with all principles
Documentation: Privacy notices, consent forms, DPIAs, audit reports, breach incident logs
The data protection policy and procedures are reviewed and updated regularly

content.text: All data processing activities must have a valid legal basis under Indonesian law: Consent:

items: When required: Processing is not necessary for core educational services. Data will be used for purposes beyond education (e.g., marketing, photo/video publication, optional trips)
How obtained: Clear, specific, freely given consent through signed consent forms. Each different purpose has its own separate consent
Withdrawal: Data subjects can withdraw consent at any time. The school must then stop processing, unless another legal basis applies
Age considerations: For students under 18, parent/guardian consent is required. Parental consent is required for all data subjects under 18, as set out in UU No. 27/2022 Article 25
content.title: 14.2.2 Legal Bases for Data Processing

items: When applies: Processing is necessary to fulfill the enrollment contract or to take steps before entering a contract
Examples: Processing student academic data to provide education; processing parent contact details to communicate about student progress; processing staff data to fulfill employment contract
No consent needed: The contract basis does not need separate consent, but the privacy notice must explain the processing
When applies: Processing is required by Indonesian law or government regulation
Dapodik reporting to Ministry of Education (student enrollment, attendance, teacher assignments)
Tax reporting for staff payroll (PPh 21, BPJS)
Cambridge examination registrations (required for exam center status)
Child protection reporting to authorities (if safeguarding concern arises)
When applies: Processing is necessary for the school's legitimate interests, as long as these interests do not override the fundamental rights of data subjects
CCTV for security purposes (legitimate interest in protecting people and property)
Alumni relations for community building (legitimate interest in maintaining school community)
Internal research to improve educational quality (legitimate interest in continuous improvement)
Balancing test required: Record in writing that the legitimate interest is proportionate and does not cause unwarranted harm to data subjects

content.text: The school respects and supports the following rights of students, parents and staff: Right of Access:

items: Data subjects can request a copy of personal data held by the school
Procedure: Submit a Data Subject Access Request form to the Principal (template in Section 19)
Timeline: The school responds within 30 days. It sends a copy of the data, or an explanation if it refuses the request
Format: Data provided in commonly used electronic format (PDF) or paper copy if requested
Scope: Includes all personal data in school systems (EduNav, paper files, emails mentioning the individual)
Exceptions: The school cannot provide data that would reveal information about other people (remove or black out third-party personal data)
content.title: 14.2.3 Data Subject Rights

items: Data subjects can request correction of inaccurate or incomplete personal data
Procedure: Tell a teacher, admin staff or the Principal about the error. Provide supporting documents if available
Timeline: Corrections are made within 7 days. Complex cases may take up to 30 days
Notification: If corrected data was shared with third parties (e.g., Cambridge, Dapodik), the school tells those parties about the correction

content.text: Right to Erasure ("Right to be Forgotten"):

items: Data subjects can request deletion of personal data in certain circumstances
Data no longer necessary for original purpose (e.g., declined applicant data after 1 year)
Consent is withdrawn and no other legal basis exists
Data was unlawfully processed
School has legal obligation to retain data (e.g., student transcripts, financial records for tax audits)
Data needed for legal claims or defense (e.g., disciplinary records during appeal period)
Data is public record (e.g., published honor roll with consent)
Procedure: Requests go to the Principal. The school responds within 30 days with its decision and the reasons
Data subjects can ask the school to limit how their data is used while a dispute is resolved
Accuracy of data is disputed (restrict processing until accuracy verified)
Processing is unlawful but data subject does not want erasure
School no longer needs data but data subject needs it for legal claim
Effect: Data can be stored but not actively used. The restriction is lifted once the issue is resolved
Data subjects can request their personal data in a structured, commonly used format to transfer it to another organization
When applies: Primarily for student transfers to another school
Procedure: Request submitted to Registrar/Academic Coordinator
Format: Student academic transcript, attendance records, assessment history provided in PDF or CSV format
Timeline: Provided within 15 days to help a smooth transfer
Data subjects can object to processing based on legitimate interest (e.g., direct marketing, alumni communications)
Procedure: Send the objection to the Principal and give a reason
Effect: The school must stop processing the data, unless compelling legitimate grounds override the data subject's interests
Absolute right: For direct marketing, the school must stop immediately when a person objects (no balancing test)
Data subjects have the right not to be subject to decisions with significant effects that are based solely on automated processing

School context: This is unlikely to apply in most cases. If the school uses automated systems for significant decisions (e.g., AI-based admissions scoring), a DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) is required. In that case, human review must also be available.

content.text: The school explains clearly how it processes data at key stages of a person's relationship with the school. Admissions Stage Privacy Notice:

items: When provided: With admissions application packet
What data is collected (student and parent information on application form)
Why it is collected (to assess suitability for admission, communicate with family)
How it will be used (admissions decision process, initial enrollment setup if accepted)
Who it will be shared with (Admissions Committee, Principal, Cambridge for exam center registration if accepted)
How long it will be retained (If accepted: duration of enrollment + per retention schedule; If declined: 1 year then securely disposed)
Rights of data subjects (access, rectification, erasure)
Contact information for data protection inquiries (Principal's email and phone)
Languages: Provided in English, with a Bahasa Indonesia summary or a full translation
Acknowledgment: By signing the application form, the parent confirms that they received the privacy notice
content.title: 14.2.4 Privacy Notices and Consent Management

items: When provided: With the enrollment contract, when the student is accepted
A full description of how data is processed during enrollment (academic records, assessments, behavior tracking, health information, photo/video for educational purposes)
Legal bases (contract for educational services, legal obligation for Dapodik reporting, legitimate interest for security/quality improvement)

Third-party data sharing: the Eduversal network (for EASE assessments, DTP professional development, appraisal system) and Cambridge (for exam registrations). Also the Indonesian government (Dapodik), emergency services (if there is a medical emergency) and local authorities (if there is a safeguarding concern).
International data transfers: Cambridge systems are hosted in the UK, with GDPR-compliant data protection
Retention periods, as set in the records retention schedule
Rights of students and parents (detailed explanation of each right)

Contact information and complaint procedure. If a person is not satisfied with how data is handled, they escalate first to the Principal, then to the Board Chair. The last step is the Indonesian data protection authority (if it has been established).

items.text: Consent sections (separate from the privacy notice):
items: Photos and videos for educational purposes: Consent for classroom photos, the school website gallery, the yearbook and social media. There is an option to opt out of public sharing.
Photos and videos for marketing: Consent to use them in school promotional materials (prospectus, advertisements). This consent is explicitly separate from educational use.
Trips and activities: General consent for off-campus activities; specific consent forms for high-risk activities (see Section 15)
Medical treatment: Consent for the school clinic to give first aid and basic medical care, and for emergency medical treatment by external providers
Communication preferences: Preferred communication channels (email, WhatsApp, phone); language preference (English or Bahasa Indonesia)
Languages: Full notice provided in English and Bahasa Indonesia
Signature: The parent signs, and the student also signs if aged 12+. The signatures confirm understanding and consent.
When provided: With job offer and employment contract
Employee data collected: Personal details, qualifications, employment history, references, tax and payroll information, performance appraisals, professional development records
Background checks: Criminal record checks (police clearance), safeguarding references, qualification checks, right-to-work documents (KITAS/KITAP for expatriates)
Purpose: To fulfill the employment contract, meet payroll and tax obligations, manage performance, support professional development and meet safeguarding requirements

Third-party sharing: tax authorities (payroll reporting), BPJS (Indonesian social security) and Cambridge (for teacher training and appraisal, if applicable). Also immigration authorities (for expatriate work permits) and Eduversal (for the appraisal system and DTP platform).
Monitoring: Email and IT systems monitoring policy (see Section 21); CCTV in common areas
Retention: Employment records are kept for 7 years after separation (the end of employment). This is a requirement of Indonesian employment law.
Rights: Access, rectification (correction) and restriction. Note: legal retention requirements may limit erasure.
Background checks: Consent for the school to carry out criminal background checks and contact referees
Professional photos: Consent for staff photo on school website and ID badge
Emergency contacts: Authorization to contact designated persons in an emergency
Languages: English (all staff) + Bahasa Indonesia for local staff
Signature: Employee signature confirming understanding and agreement
When conducted: Start of each academic year (July/August)
Process:

steps: The EduNav system creates a data verification form for each family, showing their current information
Parents review the form, correct any errors and confirm their current contact details
Consent for photo/video use is renewed (a chance to change preferences)
Return signed form by Week 2 of term
Admin staff update EduNav within 1 week of receiving forms

items: Purpose: Keeps data accurate (Principle 4), renews consent every year and keeps emergency contacts reliable
Parents or staff can withdraw consent at any time. They send the Consent Withdrawal Form (template in Section 19) to the Principal.
The school confirms receipt within 3 days and carries out the withdrawal within 7 days
Examples: A parent withdraws photo consent. The school then removes the student's photos from the public school website and social media, and takes no new photos for public use.
Note: Withdrawal does not make processing done before the withdrawal unlawful. The school may keep data if another legal basis applies (e.g., contract, legal obligation).

content.text: Physical protection of paper records and storage media is the first line of defense against unauthorized access. Student Records (Paper Files):

items: Storage location: Locked filing cabinets in administrative office (not accessible to unauthorized personnel)
Key access limited to Principal, Academic Coordinator, Registrar, and designated admin staff
A key sign-out log is kept for accountability
Cabinet locked when office unattended
Organization: Files are sorted alphabetically by student name or by class/year group, with a clear labeling system
Archival records: Files of graduated students are moved to a separate secure archive room. Storage is climate-controlled to prevent deterioration.
Visitor restrictions: Visitors are not allowed in the admin office where student files are stored. The reception area is separate from records storage.
content.title: 14.3.1 Physical Security Measures

items: Storage location: A separate locked filing cabinet (not the same cabinet as student records), in the HR office or the Principal's office
Key access limited to Principal and HR Manager only
Individual staff members can request supervised access to their own file

Safeguarding files (part of the HR files): Background checks, safeguarding references and police clearances are stored in a separate locked compartment inside the HR cabinet. Access is limited to the Principal and the DSL.
Separation principle: Current staff files are kept separate from former staff files (retention as set in Section 14.5)

items.text: Secure storage room requirements in the Cambridge Handbook:
items: A dedicated locked room, or a locked metal cabinet in a secure room
No windows, or windows with security bars/mesh
Solid door with deadbolt lock (not standard classroom lock)
Access limited to Exams Officer and Principal only
The key is kept secure (not left in the office overnight). The combination is changed every year or after a staff role change.
Alarm system or CCTV monitoring if available
Materials covered: Question papers, answer booklets, confidential instructions, completed scripts before dispatch
Sign-in/sign-out log: Every access to secure storage is logged with the date, time, person and purpose
Examination day procedures: Materials are moved directly from secure storage to the exam room, with no stops on the way and no unsecured handling
Storage: A locked filing cabinet in the finance office. Access is limited to the Principal, the Finance Officer and authorized accounting staff.
Separation: Current-year records are in the main cabinet; records from previous years are in archive storage
Audit trail: Documents are sorted by date and by category (invoices, receipts, bank statements, payroll)
Confidential waste bins: Lockable bins in administrative areas hold documents waiting to be shredded. Each bin is clearly labeled "Confidential Waste - Do Not Throw in General Trash".
On-site shredding: A cross-cut shredder (minimum P-4 security level) is used for routine confidential documents. A staff member witnesses the shredding.
Off-site shredding service: Used for bulk disposal during the annual records purge. A certified shredding vendor provides a Certificate of Destruction.
No salvage: Confidential documents must never be put in general trash or recycling bins, or given away, even if "unwanted"
Staff must not leave confidential documents on desks when they are away from their workspace
Documents are returned to secure storage or a locked drawer at the end of each day
Computer screens are locked when the user is away from the desk (automatic screen lock after 5 minutes of inactivity)
Whiteboards with student/staff information are erased before the room is left open to visitors
All visitors sign in at reception. They receive visitor badges and wear them at all times.
Visitors are escorted by a staff member. They are not left alone in areas with access to confidential information.
The visitor log is kept for 1 year as a security audit trail

content.text: Cross-reference: Section 10 (Cambridge Examinations Management - secure materials storage and handling procedures in detail), Section 15 (Risk Management - physical security risk assessments)
Full technical safeguards protect electronic data in all school systems. EduNav School Information System (SIS) - Security Architecture:

items: Teachers: View and edit data only for students in their assigned classes; cannot access other teachers' class data
Subject Leaders/Heads of Department: View data for all students in their subject across year groups; edit permissions for curriculum planning and assessment coordination
Academic Coordinator/Principal: Full view access across all students and all academic data; edit permissions for exceptional circumstances only
Parents: View-only access to their own child's data (grades, attendance, behavior, announcements); cannot see other students' data
Students: View-only access to their own data (assignments, grades, calendar); age-appropriate access (limited for younger students)
Admin Staff (Registrar, Admissions): Full edit access for enrollment, demographic data, and attendance; no access to confidential safeguarding notes or teacher appraisal data
IT Manager/Dapodik Operator: System administrator access for technical configuration; audited "view only" access to data content (not routine access)
Password requirements: Minimum 12 characters; must include uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols; no dictionary words or personal information
Password expiry: Staff passwords expire every 90 days; parents/students every 180 days
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Enabled for all admin-level accounts (Principal, IT Manager, Registrar) and recommended for all staff. Verification is by SMS or an authenticator app.
Account lockout: After 5 failed login attempts, the account is locked for 30 minutes. After 3 lockouts, the user must contact the IT Manager for a manual unlock.
Password reset process: Parents/students reset their own passwords through email verification. IT Manager approval is required for staff password resets, to prevent social engineering.
Session timeout: Automatic logout after 30 minutes of inactivity
Concurrent sessions: If a user logs in from a new device, they are logged out of the old session (this prevents shared credentials)
Secure logout: Users must explicitly log out when using shared or public computers
In transit: All data sent between the user's device and the EduNav server is encrypted with TLS 1.3 (minimum TLS 1.2). HTTPS is enforced (no HTTP access).
At rest: Sensitive fields in the database are encrypted (student health information, staff salary details, safeguarding notes). The EduNav server uses full disk encryption.
Backup encryption: All backup files are encrypted before storage. Encryption keys are managed separately from backup data.
Actions logged: All user logins, data edits (who changed what and when), data exports/downloads, permission changes, failed login attempts
Log retention: Audit logs are kept for 2 years and archived to secure storage
Log review: IT Manager reviews audit logs quarterly for anomalies (unusual access patterns, unauthorized data downloads, repeated failed logins)
Alerting: Automated alerts for high-risk activities (admin account created, bulk data export, access to safeguarding records)
Backup frequency: Daily incremental backups; weekly full backups
Backup location: An on-site backup (encrypted external drive in secure storage) and a cloud backup (encrypted, stored in an Indonesian data center for data sovereignty)
Backup testing: A monthly check that backups can be restored, and a full disaster recovery test every year
Retention: Daily backups are kept for 30 days, weekly backups for 12 months and annual backups for 7 years

content.text: Dapodik and SIMPKB Systems - Government Data Security:

items: The Principal designates the Dapodik Operator (usually the IT Manager or a senior admin staff member)
Single operator account per school (no shared credentials)
The operator attends government-certified Dapodik training every year, including a data security module
Dapodik software is installed on a dedicated computer (not a teacher's personal laptop)
The computer is in a secure office (not an area open to the public)
Physical security: The computer is locked or logged out when the operator is away from the desk
No remote access to Dapodik database from outside school network (government security requirement)
Weekly online synchronization between local Dapodik database and Ministry servers
Verification prompts are reviewed carefully before the sync is confirmed (so that no records are deleted by accident)
Sync logs are saved as PDF for the audit trail
The Dapodik operator makes a manual backup before each synchronization (in case the sync causes errors)
Backup files are stored on an encrypted external drive and kept in secure storage, separate from the Dapodik computer
Backup retention: Current semester backups + previous 2 semesters (18 months total)
The Dapodik computer is connected to a dedicated VLAN (virtual LAN), separate from the general student/staff WiFi
Firewall rules allow the Dapodik computer to communicate only with Ministry servers and the internal school network
Antivirus and anti-malware software is updated weekly, with a full system scan every month

content.text: Cambridge Examination Systems - Compliance with Cambridge Security Standards:

items: Access limited to Exams Officer and Principal only
The Centre number and access codes are stored in an encrypted password manager (not written down or saved in browser autofill)
Passwords are changed at least every 6 months, and immediately when there is a change in the Exams Officer role
Two-factor authentication is enabled (Cambridge requires it for all Centres)
Administrative access limited to Principal (Centre Head)
Used for secure materials tracking, Centre updates, incident reporting
Accessed only from school computers, not from personal devices or public WiFi
Access is given to the Principal, Academic Coordinator and Subject Leaders
Read-only access, for data analysis. No personal candidate data is downloaded or shared outside the school.
Access is removed at the end of each exam cycle. It is renewed for the next cycle after Cambridge confirms.
All Cambridge system passwords are stored in the school's password manager (for example, LastPass for Teams or Bitwarden Enterprise)
The password manager account is protected by a master password. Only the Principal and IT Manager know it.

Emergency access procedure: The Board Chair holds a sealed envelope with the password manager recovery codes. The envelope is opened only if the Principal and IT Manager are both unavailable at the same time.
All staff and students (Grade 6+) get school email accounts (domain: @schoolname.sch.id)
Personal email is not used for school business, for reasons of data protection and professionalism
The IT Manager sets up and closes email accounts. An account is turned off immediately when a staff member or student leaves.
TLS encryption protects email while it is sent (this stops interception)
Sensitive attachments (student medical records, staff HR documents) are sent as password-protected ZIP files or by a secure file-sharing link. They are not sent as unencrypted email attachments.
The password is sent by a separate channel (for example, a phone call or SMS)
Yearly staff training on how to spot phishing emails (see Section 14.9)
Email security gateway with spam/phishing filters
Staff are told never to click links or download attachments from unknown senders
Verification protocol: If an email asks for sensitive data or an urgent money transfer, check the request by phone. Call a known number, not the number in the email.
Staff email accounts: Emails are kept for 2 years in the active mailbox. They are then archived for an extra 5 years. This makes 7 years of retention in total, in line with employment records.
Student email accounts: Kept during enrollment + 1 year. Then archived for 2 years (total 3 years).
Safeguarding-related emails: Forwarded to the DSL's secure folder. Kept according to the safeguarding retention schedule (see Section 14.5).
Automatic deletion: Emails older than the retention period are deleted from the archive automatically
Enterprise-grade firewall protecting school network
Network segmentation (separate network sections): Admin VLAN (principal, HR, finance), Teacher VLAN, Student VLAN, and Guest WiFi (kept separate from the school network)

content.text: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a structured process. It finds and reduces data protection risks that come from new or changed data processing. DPIAs are required when processing is likely to cause high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. This follows UU No. 27/2022 (Indonesian Personal Data Protection Law) and international best practice (GDPR). When DPIAs Are Mandatory: Schools must carry out a DPIA before they start processing that involves:

steps: Systematic and extensive evaluation or scoring: automated decision-making systems that strongly affect people (e.g., AI-based admissions scoring, automated prediction of student performance)

steps.text: Large-scale processing of special category data:
items: Medical or health information about multiple students (e.g., a school-wide health screening database, a central medical records system)
Biometric data (fingerprint scanners for attendance, facial recognition systems)
Safeguarding or child protection data (especially if it is shared with more than one agency)

steps.text: Systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas:
items: CCTV systems that cover large parts of the school site
Systems that monitor internet activity (more than basic filtering)
Location tracking systems for student buses or devices

steps.text: New technology that could affect privacy:
items: Cloud-based learning platforms that process data on student behavior
AI tutoring systems that analyze how students learn
Exam supervision (proctoring) software for online exams (video or audio recording)

steps.text: Sending data to other countries that do not have adequate data protection:
items: Sharing student data with international educational partners outside Indonesia
Using cloud services with servers in countries that have no data protection laws
Note: Transfers to Cambridge (UK) are acceptable because of UK GDPR adequacy

steps.text: Data processing on a large scale:
items: Combining databases across the school, affecting more than 500 students
Sharing data across the Eduversal partner school network
Data analysis projects that use student records from more than one year

content.title: 14.4.1 Purpose and Legal Basis

content.text: When DPIAs Are Recommended (Not Mandatory but Best Practice):

items: Using a new outside (third-party) data processor, especially for sensitive educational services
Major changes to existing high-risk processing (e.g., expanding CCTV coverage, adding new modules to EduNav)
Combining data sets in new ways (e.g., linking academic results with behavior incident records to make predictions)
Processing data about vulnerable groups (young children, students with special needs) in new ways

content.text: The school follows a seven-step DPIA process: Step 1: Describe the Processing Activity A full description of the data processing, including:

items: Purpose and context: Why is this processing needed? What problem does it solve? How does it fit the school's educational mission?
Nature of processing: What personal data is collected? From whom (students, staff, parents)? How is it collected (forms, sensors, third-party import)?
Scope: How many people are affected? Over what time period? In what geographic area?
Data lifecycle: How is data stored? Who has access? How long is it kept? How is it disposed of?
Technology: What systems or platforms are used? Is it cloud-based or on the school's own servers (on-premises)? Who is the vendor (if any)?
content.title: 14.4.2 DPIA Process and Methodology

content.text: Example: "Installing a CCTV system covering the school entrance, corridors, playground, and parking area. Purpose: Security and safety monitoring; incident investigation; visitor management. Data: Video footage showing the faces of students, staff, parents, and visitors. Technology: 24 HD cameras connected to a digital video recorder (DVR) with 90-day storage. Access: Principal, Security Officer, IT Manager for incident review only." Step 2: Assess Necessity and Proportionality Check carefully whether the processing is justified:

items: Necessity test: Is this processing necessary for the purpose? Could the purpose be reached in a less intrusive way?

items.text: Alternative analysis: What other options were considered? Why were they not enough?
items: Example: For CCTV, alternatives might include more security staff or visitor sign-in logs. CCTV was chosen because it gives continuous monitoring and evidence for incident investigation. Human monitoring cannot match this.
Proportionality test: Is the processing proportionate to the purpose? Is the benefit greater than the privacy intrusion?
Benefits: Which risks does it reduce? What does it improve in school operations?
Privacy intrusion level: How much personal data is involved? How sensitive is it? How many people are affected?
Balance assessment: Do the benefits clearly justify the intrusion?
Surveys of students and parents about privacy concerns (especially for monitoring systems)
Staff feedback on data processing that affects them
Advice from the Data Protection Officer or a legal advisor if the issues are complex

content.text: Step 3: Identify Data Protection Risks Find the risks to individuals' rights and freedoms, one by one: Risk Categories: For each risk found, record:

content.title: DPIA Risk Categories and School-Context Examples
rows: Data accessed by unauthorized persons internally or externally
CCTV footage leaked online; student medical records accessed by unauthorized teacher
Data lost due to technical failure, human error, disaster
Server failure deletes all student records; backup incomplete
Data changed without authorization, affecting integrity
Grades altered by unauthorized person; Dapodik data corrupted during sync
Data used for purposes beyond original intent
CCTV footage used for staff performance monitoring rather than security only
Excessive monitoring creates chilling effect on behavior
Extensive monitoring makes students/staff feel constantly watched, affecting wellbeing
Automated decisions or profiling lead to unfair treatment
AI admissions system discriminates against certain demographic groups
Student ID numbers and dates of birth used for fraudulent accounts
Data breach or misuse damages individual's reputation
Data misuse leads to physical safety risk
Safeguarding data given to the perpetrator; student location tracking misused by an unauthorized person

items: Risk source: What could cause this risk? (human error, a weakness in the system, deliberate harmful action)
Likelihood: How likely is this risk to occur? (Low / Medium / High)
Severity of impact: If the risk happens, how serious is the harm to individuals? (Low / Medium / High)
Risk rating: Combination of likelihood and impact (Low, Medium, High, Critical)

content.text: Example Risk: "Unauthorized access to CCTV footage - Medium likelihood (footage is on a network-connected DVR with password protection but no encryption, so hacking is possible). High severity (the footage includes children; disclosure could cause reputational harm, or a safety risk if used for stalking). Overall risk rating: HIGH." Step 4: Identify Mitigation Measures For each risk found, name controls that reduce its likelihood or impact: Technical Controls:

items: Encryption (data at rest and in transit)
Access controls (role-based permissions, multi-factor authentication)
Audit logging (records who looked at which data, and when)
Backup and recovery systems (protect against data loss)
Anonymization or pseudonymization (makes data less sensitive)
Automatic deletion of data after the retention period ends (storage limitation)
Policies and procedures (clear rules for data handling)
Staff training (so staff understand and follow security practices)
Privacy by design (build privacy protection into the system from the start, not add it later)
Data minimization (collect only essential data fields)
Vendor checks (due diligence) for third-party processors
Incident response procedures (fast action if a breach happens)
Secure storage (locked cabinets, restricted access rooms)
Visitor management (prevent unauthorized physical access)
Clean desk policy (do not leave confidential documents out in the open)
Secure disposal (shredding, device destruction)

content.text: Example Mitigation for CCTV Risk: "1. Turn on DVR encryption for stored footage. 2. Change the default admin password to a strong password; turn on two-factor authentication if the system supports it. 3. Place the DVR in a locked server room, with an access log for the room. 4. Turn on audit logging on the DVR (it records who viewed footage). 5. Train staff on the CCTV access policy (view footage only for legitimate security incidents; no casual browsing). 6. Put up signs at school entrances to tell people about CCTV (transparency). 7. Set up privacy zones (e.g., cameras do not view inside toilets or changing areas)." Step 5: Calculate Residual Risk After mitigation, reassess the risk level:

items: Residual likelihood: With the controls in place, how likely is the risk now? (usually lower)
Residual severity: If the risk still happens despite the controls, is the impact smaller? (sometimes yes, if the mitigation includes measures that reduce impact, such as encryption)
Residual risk rating: New risk level after mitigation

content.text: Example: "Risk of unauthorized access to CCTV after mitigation: Likelihood falls to Low (encryption and strong authentication greatly reduce the risk of hacking). Severity stays High (if a breach happens, the impact is still serious). Residual risk rating: MEDIUM (acceptable with continued monitoring)." Acceptability Decision:

items: Low residual risk: Acceptable; proceed with processing
Medium residual risk: Acceptable with ongoing monitoring and regular review (e.g., an annual DPIA update)
High residual risk: May be acceptable if the benefits very clearly outweigh the risks AND no further mitigation is possible. Principal approval is required. Notifying the Board is recommended.
Critical residual risk: Not acceptable. Do not go ahead with the processing, OR put substantial extra mitigation measures in place before going ahead.

content.text: Step 6: Sign-off and Approval The DPIA is reviewed and approved by:

items: DPIA Lead (IT Manager or Project Lead): Confirms that the technical details are accurate and that the mitigation can be done
Principal (Data Controller): Approves the processing and accepts the residual risk on behalf of the school
Data Protection Officer (if designated): Reviews for legal compliance and best practice
Board Chair (for high-risk projects): Gives Board oversight of processing that has a major impact across the school or a high residual risk
Signatures with date
Any approval conditions (e.g., "Approved on condition that staff training is completed by [date]")
Review schedule (when will the DPIA be reviewed again?)
Implementation: The mitigation measures go into the project plan. They are not optional.
Ongoing monitoring: Name a person responsible for checking that the controls work (e.g., the IT Manager reviews access logs every quarter)

items.text: Review triggers: DPIA must be reviewed if:
items: Material change to processing (e.g., expanding CCTV coverage, adding facial recognition feature)
A data breach or security incident happens that is related to this processing
New legal requirements affect processing
The scheduled review date is reached (at least once a year for high-risk processing)
DPIA update: If the processing changes, the DPIA is updated and approved again. Record the changes and the reasons for them.

Example DPIA 2: EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation) Participation Description: The school takes part in the EASE digital assessment program. The Eduversal Academic Board's Subject Specialist team organizes EASE. The delivery platform is Latihan.id, run by PT. Global Zerone Digital. Students take standardized tests online. Assessment data: Test answers, scores, time spent per question, topics mastered and topics the student struggles with

Necessary: EASE gives a standard measure of student reasoning and literacy (EASE Growth) and of subject learning (EASE Assessment). EASE Growth is not tied to one curriculum sequence, and in 2026-2027 it sets a Version 1 baseline. The results inform changes to teaching and communication with parents.
Proportionate: Student-level data is necessary for individual reports. Sharing combined data to improve quality across the network is justified by the educational benefit.

steps: The vendor keeps student data longer than necessary
Vendor uses student data for commercial purposes (developing test questions, AI training)

The Data Processing Agreement states that the vendor deletes student-level data 2 years after the assessment (in line with the school assessment retention policy)
The DPA (Data Processing Agreement) prohibits the vendor from using student data for any purpose other than providing the EASE service. The vendor confirms this in an annual security questionnaire.

Anonymization protocol: If a grade has fewer than 30 students, combined data is shared only at grade level (not class level). No demographic breakdown is shared if it would allow students to be identified.
The privacy notice is updated to name EASE and data sharing with the Eduversal network clearly. The parent consent form includes a clause on EASE participation.
Training for teachers on how to share EASE results with students (focus on growth; avoid comparisons). Guidance for parents on how to read the reports.

content.text: Residual Risk: MEDIUM - acceptable with ongoing vendor monitoring. Approval: The Principal approved EASE participation with mitigation conditions. The Foundation Representative (Eduversal) confirmed the network data handling procedures. Example DPIA 3: CCTV Expansion Project Description: The existing CCTV system covers only the entrance and admin areas. The project expands it to full coverage of corridors, playgrounds, parking area, and perimeter. Upgrade to HD cameras with 90-day storage (previously 30 days). Purpose: Better security, incident investigation, visitor management. Data Processed:

items: Video footage showing the faces and activities of students, staff, parents and visitors
Audio recording is turned off (to protect privacy)
Facial recognition is not used (it would have a large extra impact on privacy)
Necessary: Past security incidents (theft, unauthorized visitor access) were not resolved because camera coverage was not enough. Manual security patrols cannot give continuous monitoring.

Proportionate: Camera placement balances security needs with privacy. There are no cameras in toilets, changing rooms, counseling offices or staff break rooms. The 90-day retention is justified by investigation timelines, because some incidents are reported weeks after they happen.
Parent survey: 78% support CCTV expansion for safety; 15% have concerns about privacy; 7% have no opinion
Student focus group (Year 9-11): Generally supportive for safety, but students ask for privacy zones (bathrooms) and no monitoring of lockers
Staff feedback: Staff support security but ask for a clear policy on footage access: only for legitimate security investigations, not for monitoring staff performance

steps: Footage is accessed for purposes other than security (e.g., monitoring staff performance, or policing minor student misbehavior)
Footage is leaked or hacked because of security weaknesses in the DVR (digital video recorder)
Too much surveillance creates a "chilling effect" on student and staff behavior and wellbeing
Keeping footage for too long increases the risk of unauthorized access or misuse
Young children (Early Years) are filmed without age-appropriate safeguards

CCTV Access Policy: A clear policy states the only reasons for viewing footage. These are: (a) investigating a security incident, (b) responding to a specific complaint, (c) safeguarding concerns. An access log is required. The Principal approves all non-emergency access. Footage is NOT used for: routine monitoring of staff performance, disciplining students for minor infractions (e.g., uniform violations), or casual browsing.

Technical security: DVR encryption is turned on. Default passwords are changed to strong passwords. Two-factor authentication is turned on. The DVR is in a locked server room with a physical access log. The network is segmented: the DVR is on a separate VLAN (virtual local area network) from the general school network.

Privacy-by-design: Signs at all entrances say "CCTV in operation for security purposes". Cameras are positioned to avoid private areas (toilets, changing rooms, medical exam spaces). Cameras are angled so they do not view inside the windows of neighboring properties.

Reduced retention: Storage is reduced from the proposed 90 days to 60 days. This balances investigation needs with the storage limitation principle. Footage is deleted automatically after 60 days, unless it is flagged for a specific incident. Flagged footage is then retained according to the retention schedule in Section 14.5.
Early Years privacy: Cameras in Early Years play areas use a "privacy mask" feature for the toileting area. CCTV does not cover the inside of Early Years classrooms (only corridor access).

content.text: Residual Risk: MEDIUM. This is acceptable with strict access controls and ongoing compliance monitoring. Approval: The Principal approved with mitigation conditions. content.text: Systematic records management means the school keeps documents for as long as they are needed. It then disposes of them securely when they are no longer needed. This balances legal compliance, efficient operations and the principle of data minimization. Key Principles:

steps: Retention for necessity: Records are kept only as long as needed for their original purpose OR as required by law
Legal compliance: Retention periods follow Indonesian regulations (education, employment, tax and archives law)
Operational access: Records are easy to find during the retention period, for operational and legal purposes
Secure disposal: When the retention period ends, records are destroyed confidentially to prevent unauthorized access
Legal holds: Disposal is stopped if records are relevant to a legal case (litigation), investigation or audit

content.text: Annual Records Review Process: Timing: Every year during the summer break (June/July), before the new academic year. Steps:

steps.text: List All Current Records (Week 1 of Summer Break):
items: Each department reviews its records (paper files, digital folders, database entries)
Compare them with the Retention Schedule to find records eligible for disposal
Create a "Records Eligible for Disposal" list with: record type, location, quantity, retention end date, disposal method required
Department Heads send their disposal lists to the IT Manager/Records Officer
The IT Manager combines the lists and checks them for accuracy

items.text: The Principal reviews and approves the disposal lists, with special attention to:
items: Safeguarding records (the DSL confirms that the records are truly eligible and that there are no ongoing investigations)
Disciplinary records (no active appeals or legal matters)
High-value contracts or financial records (confirm there are no pending audits)
Principal signs Disposal Approval Form

steps.text: Carrying Out Secure Disposal (Week 3-4): For Paper Records:
items: Gather all records approved for disposal in a secure area (a locked room or locked disposal bins)
For on-site shredding: Use a cross-cut shredder (minimum P-4 security level). The IT Manager or Records Officer supervises the shredding. Record the number of boxes/bags shredded.

For off-site shredding: A certified shredding vendor collects the sealed boxes and gives an itemized collection receipt. The vendor destroys the records and provides a Certificate of Destruction within 5 business days.
The Disposal Certificate is filed with the Principal's signature confirming completion
The IT Manager securely deletes the records using certified data erasure software (minimum 3-pass overwrite per NIST standards)
Deleted records are logged: file names, deletion date, erasure method, IT Manager signature
Backup systems: Check that deleted records are also removed from backup systems (or marked so they are excluded from future restores)
Update Records Disposal Log: Date, record type, quantity, disposal method, Principal authorization, IT Manager execution
Attach Certificates of Destruction (from shredding vendor)
The Annual Records Disposal Report is submitted to the Board/Foundation. It covers: a summary of records disposed of, compliance with the retention schedule, and any problems found.
Sample check: The Principal or an external auditor (if applicable) checks a random selection of records. They confirm that these records were properly disposed of per the schedule.
The audit result is recorded. Any differences are noted and corrected for the next cycle.

content.text: Exceptions to Routine Disposal - Legal Holds: If the school is involved in a legal case (litigation), government investigation, audit or other legal matter:

steps: Immediate hold: The Principal issues a Legal Hold Notice to all staff and the Records Officer. It says: "Do NOT dispose of any records related to [matter description] until further notice"
Scope identification: The legal advisor (or Foundation counsel) identifies the specific records relevant to the matter
Hold enforcement: The IT Manager/Records Officer makes sure the relevant records are NOT included in the annual disposal. These records are flagged in the retention system.

Hold release: When the legal matter ends (case settled, audit completed, investigation closed), the Principal issues a Hold Release Notice. The records are then disposed of under the normal retention schedule (if they are now eligible).

items.text: Extended retention: Safeguarding records about students are retained until the subject reaches age 25 (the network rule stated in 9.10 and in the schedule above). Some safeguarding records are about staff conduct toward children: allegations and the Low-Level Concern Log (T-09). These are retained for employment + 25 years after separation, as the schedule above states. The 7-year rule applies only to ordinary discipline and grievance records with no child-safeguarding element. Retention MAY need to be longer if:
items: The individual asks for the records to be retained longer (a survivor of abuse may want the school to keep records as evidence)
Ongoing police investigation or court proceedings
Historical abuse inquiry (government or institutional review of past safeguarding cases)
Disposal authority: Only the DSL or the Principal is authorized to dispose of safeguarding records. The regular Records Officer/IT Manager does NOT have this authority.
Disposal method: Safeguarding records MUST be shredded or securely deleted by the DSL/Principal personally OR under direct supervision. They cannot be included in bulk disposal with other records.
Active records (current year): Locked filing cabinets in department offices, easy to access
Semi-active records (past 1-3 years): A locked storage room next to the main office, organized in date order

Inactive records (archive - beyond 3 years): A secure archive room (climate-controlled if possible, for long-term preservation). Records are organized by year and record type. An inventory log is kept.
Permanent records (student transcripts, Board minutes): A fireproof safe or safety deposit box for the most critical records. Duplicate copies are kept in a separate secure location.
content.title: 14.5.4 Records Storage Best Practices

items: Active records: EduNav system, shared drives, department-specific folders (access-controlled)
Archived records: A separate archive database or compressed archive folders (kept out of active systems to reduce clutter)
Backup systems: Encrypted backups are kept according to the retention schedule; archived records are included in backups
Cloud vs. On-Premises: Critical permanent records (student transcripts, legal documents) are stored both on-premises AND in an encrypted cloud backup (for redundancy)
Request process: Staff who need an archived record submit a request to the Records Officer. The request states the record type, the student/staff name or date range, and the purpose of access.
Retrieval: The Records Officer retrieves the record from the archive within 3 business days. They provide a copy or supervised viewing.
Return: If a physical record is removed from the archive, a signed log is required. The record is returned within 7 days or the timeframe specified.
Digital archived records: The IT Manager can restore them from the archive system and provide read-only access or a PDF copy
