content.text: A data breach is a security incident that leads to unauthorized or unlawful destruction, loss, change or disclosure of personal data, or access to it. Breaches can come from malicious attacks, system failures or human error. Types of Data Breaches:

steps.text: Confidentiality Breach: Unauthorized disclosure or access
items: Examples: Student medical records are emailed to the wrong person. A hacker gets into the EduNav database. Paper files are left unsecured and seen by an unauthorized person. A USB drive with staff salary data is lost.

steps.text: Integrity Breach: Unauthorized alteration or corruption
items: Examples: Someone gets into a teacher account and changes grades without authorization. Dapodik data is corrupted during unauthorized access. Ransomware encrypts student records (preventing legitimate access).

steps.text: Availability Breach: Loss, destruction, or denial of access
items: Examples: A server failure deletes all student records and there is no backup. Ransomware locks the school out of its systems. A natural disaster destroys paper records that have no secure copies.

content.text:
In-Scope vs. Out-of-Scope Incidents:

In-Scope (Data Breach Response Required):

items: Any incident involving personal data (student, staff or parent names, contact information, ID numbers, grades, medical information, financial information)
Incidents affecting even a small number of people (disclosing a single student's medical record is still a breach)
Near-miss incidents with high risk (e.g., an unencrypted laptop left in a public place but recovered before anyone accessed it)

content.text: Out-of-Scope (Not Data Breach, but May Require Other Response):

items: General IT failures that do not involve personal data (internet outage, printer fault)
Physical security incidents not involving data (theft of school equipment that does not contain data)
Attempted attacks that security systems blocked successfully (phishing email caught by the filter before staff clicked)

content.text:
All staff must know: If you suspect a data breach, report it immediately. Delay increases harm.

Step 1: Detection and Immediate Notification (Within 1-4 Hours). How Breaches Are Detected:

items: A staff member notices the breach directly (e.g., sends an email to the wrong person, loses a laptop, finds unauthorized access)
IT monitoring alerts (e.g., the intrusion detection system flags suspicious activity, or an audit log review shows unauthorized access)
External notification (e.g., a vendor reports a breach, or a parent tells the school they received someone else's data)
System errors (e.g., database corruption, backup failure discovered)
content.title: 14.6.2 Immediate Response Procedure (Within 24 Hours)

steps.text: Any staff member who discovers a breach → IT Manager + Principal (immediately, even outside office hours if serious)
items: Contact methods: Phone call (do not rely on email if the email system is breached); direct message if IT systems are compromised
Information to provide: What happened? What data is involved? How many people are affected? When did it happen? Has harm already happened?

steps.text: IT Manager's first assessment (within 1 hour of notification):
items: Confirm that the breach happened (not a false alarm)
Identify the scope: what data, which systems, how many individuals
Assess ongoing risk: Is the breach still happening? Can further harm be prevented?
Activate Data Breach Response Team
Decide immediate containment actions
Notify the Board Chair if the breach is high-risk

content.text: Step 2: Containment (Within 4-12 Hours) Purpose: Stop breach from continuing; prevent further data exposure or loss Containment Actions by Breach Type: => Table <= Step 3: Initial Documentation (Within 24 Hours) IT Manager or designated staff begins Breach Incident Log (template in Section 19): Required Information:

items: Incident ID: a unique reference (e.g., BREACH-2025-001)
Detection date/time: When breach discovered
Occurrence date/time: when the breach probably happened (this may be earlier than when it was found)
Reported by: Who discovered/reported breach
Breach type: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Data involved: types of personal data (student academic records, staff salary information, parent contact details, etc.)
Data sensitivity: Low (basic contact info), Medium (academic records), High (medical, safeguarding, financial)
Individuals affected: Number and categories (students, staff, parents)
Cause: Human error, system failure, malicious attack, vendor issue
Initial containment actions: what was done to stop the breach
Current status: Contained, ongoing investigation, resolved
The Principal signs a containment confirmation within 24 hours: "Immediate actions completed; no further immediate risk"
If the breach cannot be contained within 24 hours (e.g., a complex hacking incident), record the reason and the ongoing efforts

content.text:
Step 4: Risk Assessment and Classification. Timing: the Breach Response Team completes a first risk classification within 24 hours of becoming aware of the breach. It makes the notification decision (Step 5) no later than hour 48. This way, any required notifications go out inside the statutory 3x24-hour deadline (see 14.6.4). The detailed assessment may continue after an early (preliminary) notification has been sent. Do not hold notification back to finish the full analysis. The Breach Response Team (Principal, IT Manager, Data Protection Officer if designated, relevant department head) carries out the risk analysis: Assessment Criteria:

1. Data Sensitivity Analysis: => Table <= Example Risk Assessments: Example 1: Teacher sends student grades via unencrypted email to wrong parent

items: Data sensitivity: Medium (grades are partly confidential, but not highly sensitive like medical records)
Likelihood: High (data sent to an unknown recipient; no encryption; easy to read)
Impact: Medium (embarrassment for the student whose grades were disclosed; possible family conflict; no physical safety risk)
Overall Risk: MEDIUM-HIGH RISK
content.title: 14.6.3 Risk Assessment and Classification (Initial Classification Within 24 Hours; Notification Decision by Hour 48)

content.text: Example 2: Laptop with encrypted student medical records lost in taxi

items: Data sensitivity: High (medical records are sensitive)
Likelihood: Low (device encrypted; password-protected; data not easy to access)
Impact: High IF accessed (serious privacy violation; discrimination risk) BUT the Low likelihood reduces it
Overall Risk: MEDIUM RISK (encryption greatly reduces the real risk)

content.text: Example 3: Safeguarding file left on a teacher's desk; parents could reach it during parent-teacher conferences

items: Data sensitivity: Critical (safeguarding/child protection records)
Likelihood: Medium (file possibly seen, but no confirmed access; only accessible for a short time)
Impact: Critical IF accessed (safety risk; re-traumatization; possible disclosure to the perpetrator if a family member saw it)
Overall Risk: HIGH RISK (even potential access to safeguarding records is high risk)

content.text: Example 4: Hacker accesses the EduNav database and copies out (exfiltrates) 500 students' names, grades and attendance records

items: Data sensitivity: Medium (academic records)
Likelihood: High (malicious attacker; large scale; data in the attacker's hands)
Impact: Medium (privacy violation; possible misuse for phishing; harm to the school's reputation)
Overall Risk: HIGH RISK (large scale + malicious attacker raises the risk)

content.text: Step 5: Notification Decision Matrix (Decision by Hour 48) Use the risk classification to decide the notification requirements. Make the decision no later than 48 hours after becoming aware of the breach. This way, notifications required under 14.6.4 go out within the statutory 3x24 hours:
Notification to Affected Individuals (Students, Parents, Staff): When Required:

items: High or Critical risk breaches: Always notify
Medium risk: Notify if harm is likely or the law requires it
Low risk: Generally not required unless the individual asks for it
content.title: 14.6.4 Notification Procedures

items: Preferred: Letter (physical mail, or email to a personal email address; not the school system if school email is compromised)
Urgent cases: Phone call followed by written confirmation
Large scale: individual letters plus a school-wide notice (website, newsletter)

content.text: Notification Content (Breach Notification Letter Template in Section 19): Required Elements per UU PDP No. 27/2022 and international best practice:

items: What happened (brief, non-technical explanation)
When it occurred
What data was involved (be specific, but do not cause alarm)

Example: "On June 15, 2025, a school laptop containing student records was stolen from a staff member's vehicle. The laptop contained names, student ID numbers, and academic records for 75 students in Year 9."

items.text: Realistic assessment of possible harm (do not make it seem smaller, but do not exaggerate)
items: Example: "The laptop was password-protected but not encrypted. If accessed, your child's academic information could be viewed by unauthorized persons. There is no financial information or highly sensitive medical data on this device."
Containment actions (e.g., "We remotely wiped the laptop data on June 16, 2025")
Security improvements (e.g., "All school laptops will now have full disk encryption enabled")
Example: "We immediately started a remote wipe of the stolen laptop. We are also improving our laptop security procedures to prevent similar incidents."
Practical steps to protect themselves
Examples:
"Monitor your child's school account for any unusual activity."
"If you receive suspicious emails that mention school information, do not click links or give personal information."
"Change your EduNav parent portal password as a precaution."
School contact person for questions (Principal's direct line + email)
Data Protection Officer contact if designated
Complaint/escalation information (if unhappy with the school's handling, contact the Board Chair; if still unresolved, contact the Indonesian data protection supervisory authority)
Sincere apology for the breach and the concern it caused
Assurance of the school's commitment to data protection
Statement of corrective actions to stop it happening again

Example: "We sincerely apologize for this incident and any concern it may cause. Protecting your family's personal information is our highest priority. We are adding extra security measures, including mandatory encryption and better staff training."
Clear, plain language (avoid technical terms; EAL-friendly)
Honest and transparent (do not minimize or hide facts)
Empathetic (acknowledge concern and inconvenience)
Provide in both English and Bahasa Indonesia
The DSL contacts affected families directly (this is not delegated to admin staff)
A face-to-face meeting is offered for highly sensitive cases (not just a letter)
Extra support offered (counseling referral, safety planning)
Law enforcement is notified immediately if there is a safety risk

content.text: Notification to Regulatory Authorities: Indonesian data protection supervisory authority under UU No. 27/2022:

items: When required: High or Critical risk breaches that are likely to harm people's rights and freedoms
Timeline: Within 3x24 hours of becoming aware of the breach. This applies to both the affected data subject and the supervisory authority (UU No. 27/2022 Article 46(1)).
Content: Detailed incident report (like the individual notification, but with more technical detail); the school's assessment of risk; mitigation measures; contact information
Process: Follow the procedures set by the Indonesian data protection authority (check the authority's website for current requirements)
When required: Breach involves Cambridge examination data (candidate information, exam scripts, results)
Timeline: Immediately (do not wait 72 hours)
Method: Cambridge Admin Hub incident report system + phone call to School Support Hub
Content: Full details of the Cambridge data compromised; number of candidates affected; containment actions; the school's assessment of the impact on exam security
When required: Criminal activity suspected (hacking, theft, deliberate unauthorized access)
Timeline: Immediately, once the criminal nature is confirmed
Process: File a police report at the local police station; get the report number for the records
Cooperation: Provide evidence when asked (logs, statements, affected systems for forensic analysis)
When required: A cyber insurance policy is in place, and the breach may lead to a claim (e.g., financial loss, legal costs, notification costs)
Timeline: Within the time set in the policy (usually 24-48 hours)
Content: Full incident details; estimated financial impact

content.text: Step 6: Root Cause Analysis and Corrective Actions (Within 2 Weeks) The Breach Response Team carries out a full investigation: Root Cause Identification:

items: System weakness (unpatched software, weak encryption, poor access controls)
Technology failure (hardware malfunction, software bug, backup failure)
Infrastructure weakness (network set up incorrectly, weak firewall rules)
Error (email sent to the wrong person by accident, device left unsecured, incorrect data entry)
Negligence (ignoring security procedures, using weak passwords, not locking devices)
Lack of training (staff do not know the correct procedures)
Deliberate misconduct (unauthorized access, data theft by insider) - rare but possible
Inadequate policies (security procedures not written down, or not complete)
Poor enforcement (policies exist but are not followed or monitored)
Organizational culture (security is not a priority; staff feel security measures are a burden)

content.text: 5 Whys Technique Example: Breach: Student medical records sent to wrong parent via email

steps: Why did the records go to the wrong parent? The teacher chose the wrong recipient from the email address book (similar names).
Why was the wrong recipient chosen? Email auto-complete suggested a recently used address; the teacher did not check before sending.
Why did the teacher not check the recipient? The teacher was sending routine emails; checking was not a habit; there was time pressure.
Why is checking not a habit? Staff training on email security was general. It did not stress checking for sensitive attachments.
Why was the training general? The training program was not adapted to school-specific situations and common mistakes.

content.text: Root Cause: Not enough practical, scenario-based training on email security for sensitive data. Corrective Action Plan: For each root cause, name the Corrective Actions and Preventive Measures: Extra Corrective Actions Based on Breach Type:

items: Lost/stolen devices: Make full disk encryption compulsory on ALL devices (not optional); annual physical inventory audit; GPS tracking turned on for mobile devices
Hacking/unauthorized access: Immediate security audit by an external expert; penetration testing to find weaknesses; MFA turned on for all admin accounts
Physical security: Stronger access controls; visitor badge system; enforcement of the clean desk policy; security awareness posters
Vendor breach: Review the vendor due diligence process; require annual security audits from high-risk vendors. Use more than one vendor (do not rely on a single vendor for critical systems).

content.text: Step 7: Breach Report to Board/Foundation (Within 30 Days) The Principal prepares a full Breach Report for Board/Foundation oversight: Report Structure:

items: Brief incident description
Risk level classification
Immediate actions taken
Status (resolved, ongoing monitoring, etc.)
Timeline of events (discovery, containment, notification)
Data involved and individuals affected
Cause analysis (root causes identified)
Likelihood and severity analysis
Overall risk rating
Actual harm caused (if any) vs. potential harm
Who was notified (individuals, authorities, vendors)
When notifications sent
Responses received (any complaints or concerns from affected individuals?)
Immediate containment actions
Long-term preventive measures, with a timeline for putting them in place
Responsible parties assigned
Budget implications (if security investments are required)
What worked well in response (speed of containment, effective communication)
What could be improved (earlier detection, faster notification, better training)
Policy or procedure changes needed
Principal's recommendations for Board approval (budget for security upgrades, policy changes, governance oversight)
The Board reviews the breach report in a confidential executive session
The Board approves (or changes) the corrective action plan
The Board may set up extra oversight measures for high-risk breaches (e.g., quarterly security updates to the Board for 1 year)
Board minutes record the breach discussion (confidential; not publicly disclosed)

content.text: Step 8: Update Risk Register and Documentation (Within 30 Days)

items: Risk Register: Add the data breach as a risk that has happened (realized risk); record the impact; update risk controls (see Section 15 - Risk Management)

items.text: Incident Response Log: Complete final entry in Breach Incident Log (template in Section 19):
items: Incident closure date
Final outcome: Resolved, no harm; Resolved, minor harm; Resolved, significant harm
Total cost: Direct costs (notification expenses, forensic investigation, legal fees); Indirect costs (staff time, reputational impact - estimated)
Lessons learned summary
Linked corrective actions: Reference to Corrective Action Plan
Data Protection Audit Plan: Schedule a follow-up audit to check that the corrective actions were carried out properly

content.text: Step 9: Follow-Up with Affected Individuals (If Appropriate) For High/Critical risk breaches:

items: 30 days after incident: Send follow-up communication to affected individuals
Update on corrective actions taken
Confirmation no further harm identified
Reminder of protective measures individuals can take
Contact information for ongoing questions
Renewed apology and commitment to security
Purpose: Show the school's accountability; keep trust; give reassurance
Incident Lead: Principal (overall decision-making authority)
Technical Lead: IT Manager (containment, investigation, technical corrective actions)
Notification Lead: Admissions Officer or HR Manager (draft notification letters, coordinate distribution)
Documentation Lead: Admin Staff (keep the Breach Incident Log, track actions)
content.title: 14.6.6 Breach Response Team Structure

content.text: Extended Team (Activated for High/Critical Risk Breaches):

items: Data Protection Officer: Legal compliance oversight (if DPO designated)
Legal Advisor: Foundation legal counsel or external lawyer (notification requirements, liability assessment)
Communications Lead: Marketing/PR staff (public statement if needed; media inquiries)
Department Specific Lead: Academic Coordinator (if student data), HR Manager (if staff data), Finance Officer (if financial data), DSL (if safeguarding data)
Board Chair: Governance oversight for high-risk incidents
Cybersecurity Consultant: For complex hacking incidents; forensic analysis; penetration testing after the breach
Legal Counsel: A specialist in data protection law (if there are complex legal issues or a risk of litigation)
Public Relations Firm: For major incidents requiring media management
Translator: For notification letters if there are complex language needs (beyond standard English/Bahasa Indonesia)
Timing: Once per year (during professional development week)
Participants: Breach Response Team + key staff
Scenario: A realistic breach scenario is simulated (e.g., "ransomware attack encrypts student database" or "laptop with financial data stolen")
Process:
content.title: 14.6.7 Breach Simulation and Preparedness

steps: The facilitator (IT Manager or external consultant) presents the scenario step by step (revealing information as in a real incident)
Team discusses: Who would we notify? What actions would we take? What are decision points?

content.title: 14.7.2 Data Quality Standards

content.text:
Data Quality Dimensions:

1. Accuracy: the data matches the source documents (birth certificates, teacher credentials, facility measurements)

items: Student names spelled wrongly or not matching the official ID (KTP, Kartu Keluarga)
Wrong NISN (Nomor Induk Siswa Nasional). The NISN must match the Ministry database
Teacher NIP (Nomor Induk Pegawai) or NUPTK incorrect
Wrong dates of birth (the Ministry system rejects them if they do not match the NISN)
Zero tolerance for ID number errors (NISN, NIP, NUPTK must be 100% accurate)
Names must match official government documents exactly (including spelling variations, hyphens, apostrophes)
Addresses should be detailed and match actual location (for school site verification)

content.text: 2. Completeness: all required fields are filled in. There is no missing data and there are no placeholder values

items: Using "999999" or "00000" for unknown data (Ministry flags this as invalid)
Leaving optional-but-important fields blank (e.g., parent contact info, student medical conditions)
Incomplete teacher qualification data (degrees not uploaded, institutions not specified)
100% of required fields filled in (the Dapodik software enforces this, but also validate by hand)
90%+ of recommended fields filled in (this makes the data more useful)
Zero placeholder or dummy data

content.text: 3. Timeliness: data is updated within the required time limits and shows the current status

items: New students not entered in Dapodik until weeks after enrollment (this delays NISN assignment)
Withdrawn students not removed from the system (this makes enrollment numbers too high)
Teacher departures not recorded (affects staffing analysis)
New enrollments entered within 7 days of admission
Withdrawals/transfers processed within 3 days of student departure
Teacher changes (subject assignments, departures) within 7 days
Weekly synchronization with Ministry servers (do not wait until the semester cut-off)

content.text: 4. Consistency: data is consistent inside each system and matches across systems (Dapodik vs. EduNav vs. paper records)

items: Student enrolled in EduNav but not in Dapodik (or vice versa)
Different grade levels recorded in different systems
Teacher teaching hours in Dapodik don't match actual timetable
Classroom capacity in Dapodik doesn't match actual room size
Quarterly reconciliation: Dapodik student list matches EduNav enrollment (100% alignment)
Teacher assignment hours in Dapodik match the actual teaching timetable (±2 hour tolerance for administrative differences)
Facility data (classrooms, labs) matches the physical audit (carried out annually)

content.text: 5. Validity: data follows the Ministry's data formats and validation rules

items: Invalid NISN format (it should be 10 digits; the Dapodik system rejects invalid formats)
Email addresses in wrong format (missing @ or domain)
Dates in wrong format (DD/MM/YYYY vs. YYYY-MM-DD depending on field)
Curriculum codes not matching Ministry's official list
Zero validation errors in Dapodik synchronization report
Manual check before synchronization (the Dapodik Operator reviews validation warnings)

Correct any errors; investigate warnings
Print validation report for records

Save synchronization report (PDF) for audit trail

Eduversal Partner Schools are registered Cambridge International Education Centres. They process large amounts of examination data through Cambridge's secure systems. This data comes under UK GDPR (because Cambridge operates from the UK) and under Indonesian data protection requirements. Schools therefore have dual compliance obligations. Cambridge Systems Used:

1. CIE Direct (Exam Management Portal):

items: Purpose: The main system for exam entries, candidate registrations and downloading results
Candidate personal data (full name as on ID, date of birth, gender, candidate number)
Exam entries (subjects, exam series, paper codes)
Centre information (Centre number, Centre contacts)
Special considerations and access arrangements (disability accommodations, medical circumstances)
Access control: Limited to the Exams Officer and the Principal (Centre Head)

content.title: 14.8.1 Overview of Cambridge Systems and Data Flow

items: Purpose: Centre management, secure materials tracking, incident reporting, policy updates
Centre registration information (Principal details, Centre address, contact persons)
Secure materials tracking (packet numbers, delivery confirmations)

Purpose: Post-results analysis, student performance data, subject-level statistics

School: Exams conducted per Cambridge regulations. School → Cambridge: Attendance registers, Incident reports (if any)

Cambridge Assessment International Education operates under UK GDPR. Schools must make sure they comply when they transfer student data to Cambridge. Legal Basis for Data Transfer:

1. Contractual Necessity:

items: Schools sign a Centre Agreement with Cambridge
Exam registration is a contractual obligation. Processing student data is necessary to fulfill the examination services contract.
Students/parents give consent to exam participation through the enrollment contract (see Section 14.2.4)
content.title: 14.8.2 Data Protection Requirements Under UK GDPR

items: UK GDPR applies to data processed by Cambridge in the UK

items.text: Indonesian schools transferring data to Cambridge rely on:
items: Contractual clauses: The Centre Agreement includes data protection provisions (equivalent to Standard Contractual Clauses)
Adequacy decision: The UK keeps GDPR-equivalent standards after Brexit
Parental consent: Privacy notices tell parents that data is transferred internationally to Cambridge in the UK

items.text: Schools must transfer ONLY data required by Cambridge:
items: Required: Full legal name, Date of birth, Gender, Candidate number (school-assigned)
Conditional: Special considerations/access arrangements (only if applicable - medical info, disability details)
Prohibited: Unnecessary personal data (race, religion, financial info, parent details unless specifically required for access arrangements)

content.text: Cambridge's Data Protection Obligations (Per Centre Agreement):

items: Secure storage of candidate data on Cambridge servers (encryption, access controls)
Retention limits (candidate data is kept according to the Cambridge retention schedule; typically 7-10 years for exam results and longer for certificates)
Data subject rights: Students/parents can request access to their Cambridge exam data (they send requests to Cambridge through the school)
Data breach notification: Cambridge must notify Centres within 24-48 hours if a breach affects the Centre's candidates

content.text: Centre Credentials (CIE Direct and Admin Hub): Credential Structure:

items: The Centre Number and passwords are stored in the school's password manager (e.g., LastPass for Business, Bitwarden for Teams, 1Password Business)
Only the Principal and the Exams Officer know the master password
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled on the password manager
Encrypted vault (AES-256 encryption standard)
Written on paper and kept in an unlocked drawer
Saved in an unencrypted Word document or Excel spreadsheet

Shared by email or messaging apps (even encrypted email is not recommended for long-term storage)
Primary access: Exams Officer (day-to-day exam management)
Secondary access: Principal (oversight, and emergency access if the Exams Officer is unavailable)

Temporary access: If temporary cover is needed (e.g., the Exams Officer is on leave during the exam period), the Principal grants access. The Principal removes the access immediately after the cover period.

Prohibited; each person uses own credentials where possible

content.text:
Data Entry Best Practices:

1. Accurate Data Entry:

items: Name Verification: The candidate's name in CIE Direct must match their official identification document (passport, national ID, birth certificate)
Common issues: Spelling variations (e.g., "Mohammed" vs "Muhammad"), missing hyphens (e.g., "Jean-Pierre" entered as "Jean Pierre"), extra spaces

Consequences of error: The certificate is printed with the wrong name → the candidate cannot use it for university applications → the school must request a reprint. A reprint means a delay of 6-8 weeks + a reprint fee.
Date of Birth Verification: Must match official ID. An incorrect DOB (date of birth) can cause the exam registration to be rejected.
Gender: Must match official records (M/F). Cambridge uses it for statistical analysis.
content.title: 14.8.4 Candidate Data Protection Standards

items: Schools assign candidate numbers (typically a 4-digit number in sequence, starting from 0001 each year)
Format requirements: Per Cambridge guidelines (usually numeric only, no letters)
Uniqueness: Each candidate must have a unique number within the Centre. Numbers cannot be reused, even after the candidate graduates.
Consistency: Once assigned, a student's candidate number never changes (the same number is used for all exam series while the student is enrolled)
Record keeping: Keep a Candidate Number Register (spreadsheet or database) showing: Candidate number, Student name, Year group, Date assigned, Exam series entered

content.text: 3. Special Considerations and Access Arrangements: Rules for when a candidate needs accommodations. For example: extra time for dyslexia, a reader for visual impairment, a separate room for a medical condition. Data Minimization:

items: Only submit necessary medical information: Cambridge needs to know the diagnosis and the required accommodation, not the full medical history
✅ Good: "Candidate diagnosed with dyslexia; educational psychologist report confirms 25% extra time required."
❌ Too Much: "Candidate has dyslexia diagnosed at age 8, also has ADHD treated with medication, has had counseling for anxiety, struggles in math class..."
Access arrangement requests are submitted through CIE Direct (encrypted transmission)
Supporting documents (medical reports, psychologist assessments) are uploaded as PDFs. Files are password-protected if they contain highly sensitive medical details.

After Cambridge approves access arrangements, the school deletes extra copies of medical reports. Keep one copy in the secure student file, as set out in Section 14.5. Do not keep multiple copies across different systems.

content.text: 4. Coursework and Internally Assessed Components: For subjects that need coursework to be submitted (e.g., Art & Design portfolios, Science practical assessments): Student Work Confidentiality:

items: Coursework may contain personal reflections, creative expression, or sensitive topics (especially in subjects like English Literature, Global Perspectives)
Upload security: Cambridge provides secure upload portals. Files are encrypted while they are sent.
Anonymization: Some subjects require anonymous marking. The school must follow Cambridge's anonymization procedures (remove student names from coursework and use only candidate numbers).
Moderator Access: External moderators (appointed by Cambridge) access coursework samples through a secure portal. Moderators are bound by Cambridge confidentiality agreements.

content.text: 5. Examination Scripts: After exams, completed answer scripts are processed securely: Collection and Storage Before Dispatch:

items: Scripts are collected in the exam room and placed in sealed envelopes immediately after the exam
Envelopes are stored in the secure storage room (the same room as secure exam materials; see Section 14.3.1)
Access is limited to the Exams Officer. The Principal may access it if needed.
Storage period: Typically 1-3 days, until courier collection is arranged
Scripts are sent by a Cambridge-approved courier (DHL, FedEx or another designated courier)
Tracking numbers are recorded. The Exams Officer monitors delivery confirmation.
Important: Do NOT use regular mail. Use only secure courier.
The school does NOT keep original scripts (they are sent to Cambridge for marking)
For some subjects, the school may keep photocopies of selected scripts for teaching purposes (with student consent). Anonymize them if they are used for display or sharing.
Retention period: Current academic year only. Then they are securely destroyed (see Section 14.5).

content.text:
Results Release Process:

1. Results Download (Results Day):

items: Cambridge releases results on a set Results Day (August for May/June exams, January for October/November exams)
The Exams Officer logs in to CIE Direct and downloads the results file (CSV or PDF format)
Time-sensitive: Results are typically available early morning UK time (afternoon in Indonesia because of the time difference)
content.title: 14.8.5 Results Data Handling and Confidentiality

items.text: Before giving results to students, the Exams Officer does a quick check:
items: Check that the total number of results matches the expected number of candidates
Spot-check: Check that a random sample of results (5-10 students) matches the expected subjects and levels
Flag any anomalies for investigation (e.g., a candidate missing from results, an unexpected "X" grade showing absence)

content.text: 3. Results Distribution to Students/Parents: Confidentiality Requirements:

items: Individual results are confidential: Each student receives ONLY their own results. Students cannot see other students' results.
No public display of results by name: Do NOT post a list of names with grades on the school notice board, website or social media. This violates data privacy.
Aggregate results (e.g., "School achieved 95% A-C pass rate in IGCSE Mathematics")
Anonymized examples (e.g., "A student in our school achieved 5 A grades in IGCSE")

Individual results WITH the student's explicit consent (e.g., a student agrees to be named in a school newsletter celebrating achievement). Obtain written consent first; see the template in Section 19.

content.title: Results Distribution Methods and Security Levels
rows: Preferred for IGCSE/AS/A Level results. Students or parents collect the results slip in a sealed envelope from the school office.
Results are uploaded to EduNav. Students log in with their personal login details to see their own results.
Results are sent as a password-protected PDF attachment to the student's official school email (not a personal email). The password is sent separately by SMS.
Results are mailed in a sealed envelope marked "Confidential". Suitable if the student is not reachable by other means.
Only if the parent explicitly asked for this method AND the student agrees. Use a password-protected attachment.
Avoid sending results through messaging apps. They are hard to keep secure and easy to forward by mistake.

items: Cambridge mails official results certificates to the Centre address, 4-6 weeks after results.
The Exams Officer receives the certificate packet and checks that the number of certificates matches the expected number.
Students collect certificates in person. They sign the collection log and show ID so the school can check who they are.

If the student has graduated and is not available in person, choose one option. Mail the certificate to the student's address on file (tracked mail with signature confirmation). Or keep it for the student to collect later.
Retention: The school keeps a photocopy of the certificate in the student file (see Section 14.5). The original goes to the student.

content.text: 5. Post-Results Services (Enquiries about results (EARs)): If student believes result is incorrect, school can request Cambridge review (remark, script review, clerical check): Privacy Protection:

items: The school submits EAR requests for the student. The student does not contact Cambridge directly.
Only the student's own script is reviewed. Cambridge does not share other students' scripts for comparison.
Cambridge tells the school the outcome. The school then informs the student.
If the grade changes after the EAR, Cambridge issues a revised certificate. The school gets the old certificate back from the student if possible. The school marks the photocopy "Superseded".

content.text: Legitimate Use of Results Plus: Results Plus gives useful data for school improvement, but it must be used responsibly: Acceptable Uses:

items: Internal analysis: Subject Leaders analyze grade distributions and find the topics students struggled with. They use this to inform curriculum planning.
Teacher development: Find teaching areas that need improvement and plan professional development.
Student support: Find students who need extra support in specific subjects or topics.
Reporting to Board/Foundation: Aggregate results, without identifying any individual student, for governance oversight.
Benchmarking: Compare the school's results with Cambridge global averages. Results Plus gives this comparison automatically.
content.title: 14.8.6 Results Plus Data Analysis and Privacy

items: Teacher performance evaluation based solely on results: Do not use student exam results as the sole measure of teacher effectiveness. This breaks fair appraisal principles, because many factors besides teaching affect results.
Public league tables: Do not publish school rankings of teachers by student results. They lower staff morale and break staff privacy.
Student shaming: Do not name students with low grades in public. This harms their dignity and breaks their privacy.
Export from Results Plus: Subject Leaders can export results data (Excel or CSV) for further analysis
Store files on secure school drives (not personal USB drives or cloud storage).
Password-protect files that contain identifiable student data.
Limit access to authorized staff (Subject Leaders, Principal, Academic Coordinator).
Delete files when the analysis is complete. There is no need to keep them long-term, because the original data stays in Results Plus for 12 months.
With Eduversal Foundation: Share anonymized aggregate data for network benchmarking (no individual student names; school-level data only).
With accreditation bodies (CIS/WASC): Include aggregate results in the accreditation self-study, without identifying any individual student.

With universities (for student applications): Transcripts with individual student results are provided with the student's consent, through official channels. The school registrar sends the transcript directly to the university, NOT through a Results Plus export.
Account setup: The Exams Officer creates Results Plus accounts for authorized staff (Principal, Academic Coordinator, Subject Leaders).

Role-based access: Subject Leaders get access only to their own subject's results. For example, the Math Head of Department sees only Math results. They cannot access Science results unless they also teach Science.
Access duration: Results Plus access is available for 12 months after results are released. After 12 months, Cambridge archives the data, and it is no longer available through the portal.
Account deactivation: When a staff member leaves the school or changes role, the Exams Officer deactivates their Results Plus access within 48 hours.

content.text: What Constitutes a Cambridge Data Breach: Reporting to Cambridge: Immediate Notification (Within 24 Hours): For security incidents that affect Cambridge examinations or data, school must notify Cambridge immediately: Method:

content.title: What Constitutes a Cambridge Data Breach
rows: Candidate exam results emailed to wrong student
Activate Data Breach Response (Section 14.6) + Notify Cambridge
Secure exam materials left unsecured; potentially accessed by unauthorized person
YES - Security breach (may compromise exam integrity)
Notify Cambridge immediately through an Admin Hub incident report + Lock down the materials
CIE Direct password accidentally shared with unauthorized staff member
Change password immediately + Notify Cambridge + Review access logs for suspicious activity
Candidate scripts lost in transit to Cambridge
Notify Cambridge + Notify affected students + Investigate courier issue
Student's access arrangement medical report emailed insecurely
Activate Data Breach Response + Notify Cambridge if medical info was shared with Cambridge
Teacher views Results Plus data for subjects they don't teach (curiosity)
Disciplinary action for teacher + Revoke Results Plus access + Review access controls
Exam results briefly shown on a projector during a staff meeting, with non-exam staff present
MAYBE - Depends on scope and audience
If only aggregate data was shown (no names), it is likely OK. If individual student results were visible, treat it as a breach.
Cambridge system temporarily unavailable (Cambridge server outage)
NO - Not school's breach (Cambridge IT issue)
No action required from school; wait for Cambridge to resolve

items: Primary: Cambridge Admin Hub - Incident Report Form (online submission)
Urgent/After Hours: Cambridge School Support Hub phone line (UK number; 24/7 support during exam periods)
content.title: 14.8.7 Cambridge Security Incidents and Breach Reporting

items: Centre Number and Centre name
Description of incident (what happened, when, how discovered)
Data or exams affected (which candidates, which subjects, which exam series)
Immediate actions taken (containment, affected individuals notified)
Contact person at school (Principal + phone number + email)
Cambridge confirms it has received the incident report, usually within 4 hours during UK business hours.
Cambridge investigates and gives guidance. It may require extra information from the school.

items.text: For serious breaches (exam material leakage, large-scale malpractice, significant data breach), Cambridge may:
items: Escalate to Cambridge senior management
Require a formal investigation report from the school within a set time (e.g., 14 days)
Impose sanctions (candidate disqualification, exam series cancellation, Centre suspension in extreme cases)
Notify Cambridge's Data Protection Officer (if it is a personal data breach under UK GDPR)
The school carries out an internal investigation (root cause analysis, corrective actions as set out in Section 14.6).
The school submits a formal incident report to Cambridge if requested. This is a detailed written report with evidence.
The school carries out corrective actions so the problem does not happen again.
The school tells Cambridge about the corrective actions taken. This shows that the school is actively improving security.

content.text: Exams Officer Training: Initial Training (Upon Appointment):

items: Cambridge Centre administration procedures (using CIE Direct, exam entry processes, results handling)
Secure materials handling (physical security, tracking, storage requirements in the Cambridge Handbook)
Data protection obligations (UK GDPR basics, Cambridge data sharing rules, candidate confidentiality)
Incident reporting procedures (how to recognize security breaches, reporting timelines)
content.title: 14.8.8 Staff Training on Cambridge Data Security

items: Cambridge online training modules. The Cambridge Professional Development platform offers free courses for Exams Officers.
Eduversal network training (Eduversal may organize training sessions for Exams Officers across partner schools)
Cambridge Handbook review: The Exams Officer must read and understand the Cambridge Handbook every year. A new version comes out each year.
The Exams Officer completes refresher training every year, before each exam cycle.
Focus areas: New Cambridge regulations, recent security incidents (anonymized case studies), updated procedures
The Principal attends Cambridge Centre Head briefings. These are run by Cambridge regional offices or held as online webinars.
The Principal receives updates to the Cambridge Handbook and the Centre Agreement.
The Principal signs a statement confirming that they understand the Centre Head responsibilities and data protection obligations.

items.text: Teachers who submit coursework or internally assessed work get specific training:
items: How to anonymize student work if required
Secure upload procedures (using Cambridge portals)
Deadline management (late submissions may not be accepted, and this affects student grades)
Authenticity requirements (plagiarism detection, making sure the work is the student's own)
All Cambridge-related training is recorded in staff training records (see Section 14.9).
Training completion certificates are filed in HR records.
The Exams Officer keeps a training log (courses completed, dates, topics covered).

content.text: Data protection is everyone's responsibility. Even the best technical security can fail if staff do not know the correct data handling procedures. Common causes of data breaches include:

items: Human error: Sending an email to the wrong person, leaving documents unsecured, using weak passwords
Lack of awareness: Not recognizing phishing emails, not knowing how to report security concerns, not knowing about data protection laws
Outdated knowledge: Data protection rules change over time, so staff need regular updates
content.title: 14.9.1 Rationale for Data Protection Training

steps: Awareness: All staff understand what personal data is, why it must be protected, and their legal obligations
Competence: Staff know HOW to handle data securely in their daily work (correct email use, secure file storage, good password habits)
Culture: Data protection becomes part of school culture. Staff feel confident to report concerns and ask questions.

content.text: New Staff Induction Training (Within First Month of Employment): Target Audience: All new staff (teachers, admin staff, support staff, expatriate and local staff). Duration: 90 minutes (can be split into two 45-minute sessions). Delivery Method:

items: An in-person training session led by the IT Manager or Principal (preferred, because it allows interactive discussion)
OR an online training module, if in-person training is not feasible. Staff complete the self-paced module and pass a quiz.
content.title: 14.9.2 Mandatory Data Protection Training Program

content.text: Training Content: Module 1: Introduction to Data Protection (20 minutes)

items: What is personal data? (definition, examples from school context: student names, grades, staff salaries, parent contact info)
What is sensitive/special category data? (medical info, safeguarding records, biometric data, financial data)

Why does data protection matter? (Legal obligation under UU PDP, ethical responsibility to protect privacy, consequences of breaches - harm to individuals, legal penalties, damage to the school's reputation)
Key principles of data protection (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability)

content.text: Module 2: School's Data Protection Policy (15 minutes)

items: Overview of the school's Data Protection Policy (summary of Section 14.2)
Staff responsibilities: All staff are data handlers and must follow the policy.

Privacy notices and consent: How the school gets consent, and why it is important to respect consent choices. For example, if a parent opts out of photos, the teacher must not include the child in classroom photos for the website.
Data subject rights: Students and parents can ask for their data, have errors corrected, and ask for deletion. Staff should refer these requests to the Principal.

content.text: Module 3: Secure Data Handling Practices (30 minutes) Email Security:

items: ✅ DO: Use school email for school business. Check the recipient before sending sensitive data. Use BCC for group emails to protect email addresses.
❌ DON'T: Use personal email for school work; send confidential data to the wrong person; use Reply All unnecessarily (it exposes email addresses)

Practical exercise: Scenario - "You need to send student grades to parents. How do you do it securely?" (Answer: Send a separate email to each parent with only their child's grades. Use the EduNav system if available. Password-protect the attachment if the data is highly sensitive.)
✅ DO: Use strong passwords (12+ characters, a mix of character types). Use a different password for each account. Turn on MFA where available. Use a password manager.
❌ DON'T: Use simple passwords (e.g., "password123"); use the same password for several accounts; write passwords on sticky notes; share passwords with colleagues
Practical exercise: "Create a strong password using a passphrase method" (e.g., "ILove2TeachMath@SchoolName!" - easy to remember but strong)

✅ DO: Lock your computer when you leave your desk (Windows: Windows Key + L; Mac: Control + Command + Q). Store confidential documents in locked cabinets. Shred confidential waste. Escort visitors. Report lost or stolen devices immediately.
❌ DON'T: Leave confidential documents on your desk overnight; throw confidential papers in regular trash; leave visitors unattended; delay reporting lost devices

Practical exercise: Walk through this scenario - "You're leaving your classroom for lunch. What do you do?" (Answer: Lock your computer. Secure any student work or grade sheets in your desk drawer, or take them with you. Close the door.)
✅ DO: Use a device PIN or password. Turn on full disk encryption. Keep devices physically secure (do not leave them in a car overnight). Report lost devices immediately.

❌ DON'T: Use school-issued devices for high-risk personal activities (downloading pirated software, visiting suspicious websites); store school confidential data on personal devices without authorization

content.text: Module 4: Recognizing and Reporting Data Breaches (15 minutes)

items: What is a data breach? (examples: lost laptop, email sent to wrong person, hacking incident, paper files left unsecured)
How to recognize possible breaches: If you ask yourself "Did I just accidentally expose someone's personal data?", the answer is probably yes.
IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED: Report ANY suspected breach to the IT Manager and Principal immediately (within 1 hour if possible; the same day at the latest).
Reporting is NOT optional. Delays increase the harm.
No blame culture: Accidents happen. The school needs to know quickly so it can respond well.
Reporting method: Email (if the email system is not compromised) or a phone call. Use the Breach Incident Report Form (template in Section 19), or simply describe what happened.
Open discussion: Staff ask questions about specific situations they might encounter
Scenario discussion: Present 2-3 realistic scenarios. Staff discuss the right actions.

content.text: Example Scenarios: Scenario 1: You accidentally sent a student's medical information to another parent via email. What do you do?

items: Correct Answer: 1) Immediately notify the IT Manager and Principal. 2) Email the recipient and ask them to delete the email and confirm the deletion. 3) Record the incident. 4) The school will assess how serious the breach is and decide if further action is needed (e.g., notifying the affected student's parents).

content.text: Scenario 2: A parent asks you to send them their child's grades via WhatsApp because it's faster. Can you do this?

items: Correct Answer: No. WhatsApp is not a secure, official communication channel for confidential student data. Explain to the parent that grades will be shared through the EduNav parent portal or official school email. If the parent does not have access, help them set it up. Or give them the grades in a sealed envelope when they pick up their child.

content.text: Scenario 3: You find a USB drive in the staff room with no label. What do you do?

items: Correct Answer: Do NOT plug it into your computer, because it could contain malware. Give it to the IT Manager or the Principal. They check if it contains school data and find the owner in a secure way.
End-of-training quiz (10 multiple-choice questions; passing score 80%; unlimited attempts allowed)
Quiz questions cover key concepts (what is personal data, password security, breach reporting)
Staff must pass the quiz to complete the training (this is proof that they understand it)
HR records each completion in the training register
Presentation slides (PowerPoint or PDF)
Handout: A one-page "Data Protection Quick Reference Guide" (a laminated card that staff keep at their desk)
Quiz (online or paper-based)
Certificate of completion (for staff records)

content.text: --- Annual Refresher Training (All Staff - Every Year): Target Audience: All staff (both continuing and new staff) Duration: 60 minutes Delivery Method:

items: Online training module (flexible timing; staff complete it during the set PD week in July/August)
OR a group training session during the annual staff PD day

content.text: Training Content: Module 1: Policy Updates and Legal Changes (15 minutes)

items: Any changes to the school's Data Protection Policy in the past year
Updates to Indonesian data protection law (UU PDP implementation regulations if issued)
Changes to Cambridge data requirements (if applicable)
New systems or vendors (e.g., "We now use [new EdTech platform]; here's how to handle data securely in this system")

content.text: Module 2: Lessons from Past Year's Incidents (20 minutes)

items: Anonymized case studies: Review data breaches or near-miss incidents from the past year (at the school or in the education sector in general)
Example: "Last year, a school in Jakarta experienced a data breach when a teacher's laptop was stolen. The laptop was not encrypted, and student records were exposed. What can we learn from this?"
Discussion: What went wrong? How could it have been prevented? How does our school prevent similar incidents?
Focus on learning, not punishment: "We review these incidents not to blame, but to learn and improve"

content.text: Module 3: Phishing and Cybersecurity Threats (15 minutes)

items: Phishing awareness: How to recognize phishing emails. Common signs are urgent requests, a suspicious sender, spelling errors, and requests for passwords or financial information.
Real examples: Show real phishing emails that were sent to the school (or to similar institutions), with identifying information REDACTED (removed)
What to do if you suspect phishing:

steps: Do NOT click links or download attachments
Do NOT provide personal information or passwords
Report to the IT Manager immediately. Forward the email if it is safe to do so; do not forward it if it contains malware.
Delete email after reporting

items: Ransomware awareness: A short explanation of ransomware (malware that encrypts data and demands payment). Prevention depends on not clicking suspicious links or attachments.
Social engineering: A warning about phone calls or messages from people who claim to be IT support and ask for passwords. IT never asks for passwords.
Interactive quiz or scenario-based exercise
Example: "You receive an email from 'principal@schoolname-update.com' (note: slight misspelling of domain) asking you to urgently verify your email password. What do you do?"

Correct answer: Recognize that this is phishing. The Principal would never ask for a password by email, and the domain spelling is suspicious. Do not respond. Report it to the IT Manager. Delete the email.
End-of-training quiz (shorter than the induction quiz; 5 questions; 80% passing score)
A certificate of completion is issued when the staff member passes
The HR Manager tracks annual training completion
Report to the Principal: The percentage of staff who completed the training by the deadline. Target: 100% completion within 2 weeks of the training becoming available.
Follow-up: Staff who miss the deadline receive a reminder. If they still have not completed it after 1 week, the matter is escalated to the Principal (it may become a performance issue).

content.text: --- Role-Specific Training (Advanced Training for Specific Roles): Dapodik Operator Training:

items: Frequency: Annual (government-certified training)

Duration: 2-day intensive training

content.text: Beyond formal training, the school runs ongoing awareness campaigns. They keep data protection "top of mind": Data Protection Day (Annual Event - January 28): January 28 is International Data Privacy Day. It marks the signing of Convention 108, the first international data protection treaty. School Activities: Staff Event:

items: Morning assembly/staff meeting: The Principal gives a short message (5 minutes) on why data protection matters. The Principal also recognizes staff who showed excellent data protection practice in the past year.

Lunch-and-learn session (optional): The IT Manager presents "Data Protection Tips and Tricks" (30 minutes). Topics: new security features in EduNav, how to use a password manager well, and recent phishing trends.

Data Protection Quiz Competition: A fun quiz with small prizes. The questions are about the school's data protection policy. Example: "The first staff member to answer all questions correctly wins a coffee voucher". Questions are posted on the staff notice board or sent by email.
content.title: 14.9.3 Data Protection Awareness Campaigns

items: Primary students (Years 1-6): Assembly on "Keeping Your Information Safe". It teaches students not to share passwords and not to post personal information online. It also teaches that some information is private (addresses, phone numbers, photos shouldn't be shared with strangers).

Secondary students (Years 7-12): Assembly or class session on "Digital Footprint and Privacy". It covers social media privacy settings, the risks of oversharing online, how websites and apps collect data, and how to protect personal information.

Newsletter article: "How We Protect Your Family's Data". It explains the school's data protection measures and what data is collected and why. It also explains parents' rights (access, rectification, deletion) and how to contact the school with data protection questions.
Website update: The data protection page on the school website is updated with FAQs. Examples: "How is my child's data used?" "Who has access to student records?" "How long are records kept?"
Posters: Data protection posters in the staff room, admin offices and corridors
Example messages: "Lock Your Screen When You Step Away", "Think Before You Click - Avoid Phishing", "Shred Confidential Documents, Don't Trash Them", "Confidential? Lock It!"

Email signature reminders: During Data Protection Day week, staff add a reminder to their email signature. The reminder reads: "January 28 is Data Privacy Day - Protecting Personal Information is Everyone's Responsibility"

content.text: --- Quarterly Security Tips (Email Bulletins): Frequency: 4 times per year (end of each quarter) Delivery: Email from IT Manager to all staff Content (Rotating Topics): Q1 (September) - Password Security:

items: Reminder to use strong, unique passwords
How to use the school's password manager (if provided)
Turn on MFA (multi-factor authentication) on personal accounts (bank, email, social media) for extra security
Warning about reusing passwords (if one account is compromised, the others are at risk)
More phishing emails during the holiday season (fake delivery notices, charity scams, holiday shopping phishing)
Examples of recent phishing attempts targeting schools
Reminder: Check the sender, do not click suspicious links, and report to the IT Manager

content.text: Q3 (March) - Physical Security and Clean Desk Policy:

items: Reminder to lock computers when away
Clean desk policy: Do not leave confidential documents on your desk overnight
Secure storage: Use locked cabinets for paper files
Visitor awareness: Challenge unknown people in school (politely ask if they have signed in)

content.text: Q4 (June) - Data Breach Prevention and End-of-Year Data Cleanup:

items: Reminder that the end of the academic year is the time to review and delete unnecessary data
Teachers should delete outdated student files (following the retention schedule)
Dispose of old documents securely (use confidential shredding bins)
Reminder to report any suspected breach immediately, even if it happened months ago (better late than never)
Short email (300-500 words)
Visual graphic or infographic
Quick tip or checklist
Link to extra resources (e.g., school's data protection policy, online training modules)

content.text: --- Data Protection Champions Program (Optional - for Larger Schools): Concept: Name one staff member per department as "Data Protection Champion" Role of Champion:

items: Be the first point of contact for data protection questions in their department
Promote data protection awareness among colleagues
Report data protection concerns to the IT Manager or Principal
Attend quarterly Data Protection Champions meetings (30 minutes; led by the IT Manager)
Receive slightly more advanced training (e.g., 1 extra hour of training per year on new topics)
Shared responsibility (not all questions go to the IT Manager or Principal)
Peer support (staff may feel more comfortable asking a colleague than going to management)
Continuous awareness (Champions remind colleagues of best practice in daily work)
Volunteer, or nominated by the department
Commit to 1-year term (renewable)
Recognized in the staff newsletter and given a "Data Protection Champion" certificate

items.text: Initial 2-hour training (in addition to the standard annual training) covering:
items: Detailed review of the school's data protection policy
How to answer common staff questions
When to escalate to the IT Manager or Principal (complex questions, suspected breaches)
Data protection trends and new risks
Quarterly meetings (30 minutes) for updates and discussion
