content.text: Ongoing monitoring makes sure that data protection policies and procedures are not just written documents, but are actually used and work well. Monitoring has several purposes:

steps: Compliance check: Confirm that the school meets its legal obligations (Indonesian UU PDP, Cambridge requirements, CIS/WASC standards)
Risk identification: Find weaknesses before they lead to breaches (e.g., outdated software, weak access controls)
Performance improvement: Find areas where procedures can be made simpler or better
Accountability: Show stakeholders (Board, parents, regulators) that the school takes data protection seriously
Learning culture: Regular reviews give chances for continuous learning and improvement
content.title: 14.10.1 Purpose of Data Protection Monitoring

content.text: Quarterly Access Audits (IT Manager - End of Each Quarter) Purpose: Check that user access permissions are appropriate. Find unauthorized access or dormant accounts. Audit Scope: EduNav System Access:

items: User List Review: The IT Manager produces the current user list from the EduNav admin panel

items.text: Dormant accounts: Users who have not logged in for 6+ months (except accounts for staff on approved leave)
items: Action: Disable dormant accounts; turn an account back on if the user returns and asks for access

items.text: Former staff with active accounts: Staff who have left the school but whose accounts are not yet disabled
items: Action: Deactivate the account immediately; investigate why it was not disabled during the departure process (see Section 12 - staff offboarding)

items.text: Excessive permissions: Users with admin-level access who do not need it (e.g., a teacher given the admin role by mistake)
items: Action: Lower the user to the correct role-based access

items.text: Generic/shared accounts: Accounts not assigned to a specific person (e.g., "Admin", "Guest", "Teacher1")
items: Action: Deactivate generic accounts; enforce the policy that each user has their own account

content.title: 14.10.2 Quarterly Internal Data Audits

items: Check the Dapodik Operator account: Confirm that only the designated Operator has access (no unauthorized extra users)
Password change check: Confirm that the Dapodik password was changed if the Operator role changed in the past quarter
Access logs: Review Dapodik access logs (if available) for unusual access times (e.g., 2 AM on Saturday - possible unauthorized access)

content.text: Cambridge Systems (CIE Direct, Admin Hub, Results Plus):

items: Credential holders: Check that only the Exams Officer, the Principal and authorized Subject Leaders (for Results Plus) have access
Password rotation: Check that Cambridge passwords are changed on the 6-month schedule (or immediately if the Exams Officer changes)
Access logs: Ask Cambridge for access logs if available; review them for unusual activity
User list: Check that only the Finance Officer, the Principal and the Board Treasurer (if applicable) have access
Permission levels: Confirm that read-only and edit permissions are appropriate

items.text: The IT Manager prepares an Access Audit Report (1-2 pages) that summarizes the findings:
items: Total active accounts by system
Dormant (unused) accounts are identified and action is taken
Permission discrepancies identified and corrected
Any security concerns are flagged (e.g., shared passwords, attempts at unauthorized access)
The report goes to the Principal for review and approval
The Principal signs off: "Access audit reviewed; corrective actions approved"

content.text:
Frequency: Quarterly (September, December, March, June). --- Annual Comprehensive Data Protection Audit (Principal + IT Manager + External Auditor if Available). Purpose: An in-depth review of the whole data protection program. It checks compliance with policies and regulations and finds improvements for the whole system. Audit Scope:

1. Policy Compliance Review:

items: Current policies: Check that all data protection policies are up to date (Data Protection Policy, Privacy Notices, Retention Schedule, Breach Response Procedure)
Legal alignment: Confirm that the policies match current Indonesian law (UU PDP and its implementing regulations), Cambridge requirements and CIS/WASC standards
Policy communication: Check that staff can access the policies (on the staff portal and referenced in the staff handbook)

Policy awareness: Survey a sample of staff (5-10 staff, chosen at random): "Have you read the school's Data Protection Policy? Can you name 3 key principles?" The survey checks awareness; it is not a punishment.
Systems inventory: List all systems that process personal data (EduNav, Dapodik, SIMPKB, Cambridge, Email, Cloud Storage, Financial System, CCTV, etc.)
Data flow mapping: For each system, record the following. What data is collected → how it is processed → where it is stored → who has access → how long it is kept → how it is disposed of
Third-party processors: Check that all vendors that process school data have valid Data Processing Agreements (see Section 14.3.5)
New systems: Identify any new systems introduced in the past year. Confirm that DPIAs were carried out if required (see Section 14.4)
Sample check: Choose 20-30 records at random from different categories (student files, staff files, financial records)
Are records kept for the correct period under the Retention Schedule (Section 14.5)?
Are records disposed of properly when the retention period ends?
Check disposal logs: Review the Records Disposal Log (Section 14.5.5). Check that disposals are documented and approved by the Principal
Shredding vendor certificates: Check that Certificates of Destruction were received for all off-site shredding (Section 14.5.3)
Request log review: Review Data Subject Request Log (Section 14.2.3)
Response timeliness: Check that requests were answered within the required timelines (30 days for access requests, 7 days for rectification)
Request fulfillment: Take a sample of 2-3 requests. Check that the responses were appropriate and complete
Incident log review: Review Breach Incident Log (Section 14.6.2)

items.text: Response effectiveness: For each breach in past year, evaluate:
items: Was breach detected promptly?
Was containment effective?
Were notifications sent to the affected people and the authorities as required?
Were corrective actions implemented?
Lessons learned documented?

Trends analysis: Do certain types of breach keep happening? For example, several emails sent to the wrong person suggest a need for better training or technical controls, such as email confirmation prompts.
Training completion rates: Review Staff Training Register (Section 14.9.4)
Check that 100% of staff completed induction training
Check that 100% (or near 100%) of staff completed annual refresher training
Identify any staff who have not complied; escalate to HR/Principal
Training effectiveness: Review average quiz scores. If they are consistently low, consider revising the training content or the way it is delivered

items.text: System security settings: Check the security settings on key systems (EduNav, Dapodik, Email):
items: Password policies are enforced (minimum length, complexity, expiration)
Multi-factor authentication is enabled for admin accounts
Encryption is enabled (data at rest and in transit)
Backup verification: Test restoring data from backups (Section 14.3.2). Confirm that backups can be recovered within an acceptable time (RTO - Recovery Time Objective)
Vulnerability scan: If the budget allows, carry out an external penetration test or vulnerability scan. Review the results and prioritize the fixes
Patch management: Check that all systems have the latest security patches installed
Filing cabinets (locked? Keys secured?)
Secure storage room for exam materials (Does it meet Cambridge requirements? Is an access log kept?)
Server room or IT equipment room (Is it locked? Is it climate controlled? Is there fire suppression?)
Confidential waste bins (Are they locked? Are they emptied regularly?)
Visitor management: Review visitor logs. Check that all visitors signed in and out and that visitor badges were used
Vendor list: Confirm list of all third-party data processors (Section 14.3.5)
DPA review: Check that Data Processing Agreements are in place and current for all vendors
Vendor security questionnaires: Check that vendors completed their annual security questionnaires (Section 14.3.5)
Vendor incidents: Review any incidents that vendors reported in the past year. Assess how the school responded
Evidence mapping: Check that data protection evidence matches the CIS/WASC accreditation standards (Section 14.11 - Compliance Alignment)
Evidence availability: Confirm that the required evidence documents are easy to find and well organized (for an accreditation self-study or site visit)

items.text: Format: A full written report (10-15 pages) with:
items: Executive summary (1 page): Overall compliance status, key findings, priority recommendations
Detailed findings by audit scope area (Sections 1-10 above)
Risk rating for each finding (Low, Medium, High, Critical)
Recommendations with action owners and target completion dates
Positive findings (areas of strong compliance), not just weaknesses
Delivery: The report is presented to the Principal. A summary is presented to the Board at a governance meeting
Follow-up: An action plan is developed to address the audit recommendations. Progress is tracked quarterly
If the school budget allows, bring in an external data protection auditor or consultant to carry out the annual audit (this gives an independent view)
The external auditor has no conflict of interest and can assess the school's practices objectively
An external audit report carries weight with regulators, accreditation bodies and parents (it shows transparency)

content.text: Frequency: Annual (usually during the summer break - June/July - when it disrupts school operations less)
Automated Security Monitoring: Antivirus and Malware Protection:

items: Real-time scanning: Antivirus software runs all the time on all school computers and scans files as they are opened
Daily signature updates: Antivirus definitions are updated daily to detect the latest threats
Weekly full scans: Automatic full system scans are scheduled for all computers (usually overnight or at the weekend)
Quarantine alerts: The IT Manager receives email alerts when malware is detected and quarantined
Monthly reports: The IT Manager reviews antivirus reports and identifies any computers with repeated infections. These may show a user behavior risk or a need for reimaging
content.title: 14.10.3 System Security Monitoring

items: Network traffic monitoring: The IDS monitors network traffic for suspicious patterns (port scans, brute-force login attempts, unusual data transfers)
Automated alerts: The IT Manager receives alerts for high-priority events. An example is multiple failed login attempts from an external IP address, which is a possible hacking attempt
Log review: The IT Manager reviews firewall and IDS logs weekly (30-45 minutes) to find anything unusual
Blocked connections: Review the list of blocked connection attempts. Check that the firewall rules work
Spam and phishing filter: The email gateway filters out spam and known phishing emails before they reach user inboxes
Quarantine review: The IT Manager reviews quarantined emails weekly. Sometimes real emails are flagged by mistake; release them to the recipient if they are safe

items.text: User-reported phishing: When staff report suspected phishing (Section 14.9.2), the IT Manager investigates:
items: Verify if phishing attempt
Block sender if malicious
Send an alert to all staff if there is a widespread phishing campaign targeting the school
Automated daily backups: EduNav, Dapodik, the Financial System and File Servers are backed up daily (automated process)
Backup success notifications: The IT Manager receives a daily email confirming that the backup was completed successfully
Monthly restoration tests: The IT Manager does a test restoration from backup. The IT Manager selects a small data set at random, restores it to a test environment and checks that the data is intact

Annual full disaster recovery test: The IT Manager simulates a major system failure. The IT Manager then fully restores a critical system (e.g., the entire EduNav database from backup). The IT Manager checks that the restoration time meets the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) target
Automated updates: Windows Update (or the equivalent for another OS) is enabled for automatic security patches on most systems
Monthly patch review: The IT Manager reviews patch logs and confirms that critical security patches are installed
Application updates: The IT Manager manually updates applications that automated updates do not cover (EduNav, Dapodik, specialized software)
Update testing: For major updates (e.g., an EduNav version upgrade), the IT Manager tests in a non-production environment before deploying to production. This avoids breaking functionality

content.text: Indonesian Regulatory Monitoring: Challenge: Indonesian data protection law (UU PDP No. 27/2022) is fairly new. Its implementing regulations are being developed step by step. Monitoring Process:

items: Legal advisor (if available): The school's legal counsel or the Foundation legal team monitors regulatory developments. They give updates to the Principal when new regulations are issued

Government websites: The IT Manager or Principal checks the Komdigi website from time to time for UU PDP updates (https://www.komdigi.go.id/). Komdigi is the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs, formerly Kemkominfo

Professional networks: The Principal takes part in Indonesian school leadership associations (e.g., ASPENSI - Indonesian Private School Association). Regulatory updates are often shared through these networks
Eduversal network: The Eduversal Foundation monitors regulatory changes that affect partner schools and gives briefings to school Principals
content.title: 14.10.4 Compliance Monitoring and Regulatory Updates

steps: Legal review: The Principal (with the legal advisor if available) reviews the new regulation and assesses its impact on the school
Gap analysis: Compare the school's current practices with the new requirements; identify the gaps
Action plan: Develop an action plan to achieve compliance. Assign responsibilities and deadlines
Policy update: Update Data Protection Policy and related procedures to reflect new requirements
Staff communication: Brief staff on new requirements and any changes to procedures
Documentation: Record compliance efforts (evidence for audits and accreditation)

content.text: Cambridge Requirements Monitoring: Cambridge Handbook Updates:

items: Cambridge publishes an updated Cambridge Handbook every year (usually in January/February for the coming exam year)
The Exams Officer and Principal receive a notification from Cambridge and download the new Handbook
Review process:

steps: The Exams Officer reads the new Handbook and highlights changes from the previous version
The Exams Officer prepares a summary of the changes (1-2 page memo)
The Principal reviews the summary and approves any procedural changes needed to comply
The Exams Officer makes the changes and updates the school's exam procedures documentation (see Section 10)

items: Staff training: If the changes are significant, the Exams Officer runs brief training for staff involved in exams (invigilators, Subject Leaders)
CIS and WASC update their accreditation standards from time to time (typically every 5-7 years)
Monitoring: The school's Accreditation Coordinator follows CIS/WASC communications and attends CIS/WASC webinars and conferences
Impact assessment: When new standards are released, the Accreditation Coordinator reviews their impact on the school and identifies new evidence requirements
Data protection intersection: New standards can affect data protection or technology domains. If they do, the Principal and IT Manager take part in the gap analysis and action planning
Ongoing alignment: The annual data protection audit (Section 14.10.2) includes a CIS/WASC readiness check. This keeps data protection evidence current and well documented

content.text: Data Protection Committee (Optional - For Larger Schools): Purpose: An oversight body for the data protection program. It provides governance and strategic direction. Composition:

items: Chair: Principal
Members: IT Manager, HR Manager, Academic Coordinator, Data Protection Officer (if designated), Foundation Representative (Eduversal)
Frequency: Quarterly meetings (60-90 minutes)
content.title: 14.10.5 Continuous Improvement Process

items: Review quarterly access audit reports; discuss the findings and approve corrective actions
Review data breach incidents (if any) and corrective action plans
Discuss emerging data protection risks and trends (new technologies, new threats, regulatory changes)
Approve major data protection initiatives (new systems, policy updates, DPIA outcomes)
Monitor action items from the annual data protection audit and track their completion
Review the data protection training program; approve updates or improvements
Meeting agendas and minutes maintained
The action item log tracks assigned tasks, responsible people, target dates and completion status
Minutes are submitted to the Board quarterly (as part of the Principal's report)

items.text: Annual staff survey (anonymous): Include questions about data protection:
items: "Do you feel confident handling student/staff data securely?" (Likert scale 1-5)
"Have you encountered any data protection challenges in your work? Please describe." (Open-ended)
"What extra training or support would help you manage data more securely?" (Open-ended)
Survey results: The IT Manager and HR Manager analyze the results and identify common concerns or suggestions
Action: Based on the feedback, adjust the training program, clarify procedures and provide extra resources

items.text: Privacy notice feedback: When parents receive privacy notices (Section 14.2.4), include a way to give feedback:
items: "Do you have any questions or concerns about how we use your family's data? Contact [Principal email]"

items.text: Annual parent survey: Include data protection question:
items: "Do you trust that the school protects your family's personal information?" (Yes/No/Unsure + optional comment)

Parent-Teacher Conferences: Teachers may hear data protection concerns from parents during conferences. For example: "I received my neighbor's child's report card by mistake" - this is a breach! Teachers report these concerns to the Principal
Student council: Data protection is discussed from time to time in student council meetings. Student representatives can share concerns from other students

Digital citizenship lessons: Teachers who deliver the digital citizenship curriculum may receive student questions about the school's data practices. Note common questions and answer them in future lessons or FAQs
Encourage staff to report near-miss incidents (e.g., "I almost sent a confidential email to the wrong person but caught it just in time")
Near-miss reports are analyzed for trends, and preventive measures are put in place
Staff who report near-misses or suggest security improvements are recognized positively. They are not punished for honest mistakes

content.text: --- Benchmarking and Best Practice Adoption: Eduversal Network Sharing:

items: The Eduversal Foundation holds meetings of school Principals and IT Managers across partner schools from time to time
Data protection topics are discussed. Schools share best practices, lessons learned from incidents and effective training methods
Example: "One partner school implemented email confirmation prompts that reduced misdirected emails by 90%; other schools adopt same solution"
Principal and IT Manager take part in international school associations (e.g., CIS regional meetings, ECIS - European Council of International Schools conferences)
Sessions on data protection, cybersecurity and GDPR compliance give insights from schools worldwide
Adapt international best practices to Indonesian context
IT Manager attends data protection conferences or webinars (e.g., IAPP - International Association of Privacy Professionals)
Stays current on emerging threats (ransomware trends, new phishing techniques)
Puts preventive measures in place early (before the school is affected)
Evaluate new security technologies from time to time (e.g., advanced email filtering, endpoint detection and response software, data loss prevention tools)
A business case for technology improvements is presented to the Board (cost compared with risk reduction benefit)
Improvements are put in place in phases, based on priority and budget

content.text: --- Annual Data Protection Improvement Plan: Process:

steps.text: End of academic year (May/June): The IT Manager and Principal review the past year's data protection activities:
items: What went well? (successes to celebrate and sustain)
What challenges did we meet? (incidents, audit findings, staff feedback)
What can we improve? (new technologies, emerging risks, best practices from other schools)

steps.text: Develop Improvement Plan: Use the review to set 3-5 priority goals for the next academic year

items: Goal 1: Reduce email security incidents by 50% through better email confirmation prompts and targeted training
Goal 2: Reach 100% DPA coverage across all vendors. Currently 85% have DPAs; the other 15% are older vendors that still need agreements
Goal 3: Turn on multi-factor authentication for all staff accounts in EduNav (currently only admin accounts have it)
Goal 4: Carry out the school's first external data protection audit (hire an external auditor)
Goal 5: Write a student data protection curriculum for Years 7-9 (with a focus on digital citizenship)

steps: Resource allocation: For each goal, list the resources needed (budget, staff time, outside support)
Approval: The Improvement Plan is sent to the Board for approval and budget allocation
Implementation: Work toward the goals during the academic year. Track progress every quarter (through the Data Protection Committee, if the school has set one up)
Year-end review: In the following year, check whether the goals were met. Celebrate successes and identify work that continues

items: Data protection is not "set and forget". It needs constant attention and change
Threats keep changing (new cyberattacks, new technologies, new regulations)
The school's data protection program must change with them
Culture of continuous improvement: "We can always do better. We learn from incidents and near-misses. We act before problems happen."

content.text: To comply with Indonesian regulations, schools must refer to specific laws and regulations. The key legal references for data protection are below. Primary Legislation:

steps.text: UU No. 27/2022 tentang Pelindungan Data Pribadi (Personal Data Protection Law)
items: Enacted: October 17, 2022
Effective: October 17, 2024 (2-year grace period for implementation)
Article 17-19: Data protection principles (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, accountability)
Article 20-21: Legal bases for processing (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public interest, legitimate interest)
Article 33-40: Rights of the data subject (the person the data is about): access, rectification (correction), erasure, restriction, portability, objection
Article 42-43: Security obligations of data controllers and processors
Article 44-45: Data processor agreements, data sharing requirements

Article 46: Data breach notification duties - written notice within 3x24 hours to the data subject and to the supervisory authority. (Articles 56-59 cover cross-border transfer, not breach notification.)
Article 60: Accountability and documentation obligations

Status of implementing regulations: As of 2025, the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology is developing implementing regulations. They cover specific topics, such as breach notification procedures and DPIA requirements. Schools should monitor for updates

steps.text: UU No. 35/2014 tentang Perubahan atas UU No. 23/2002 tentang Perlindungan Anak (Child Protection Law)
items: Provisions relevant to data protection: protecting children's privacy, and special care when processing children's data (parental consent for children under 18)
Requires government and educational institutions to keep proper records management systems
Sets retention requirements for official records (they vary by record type)

steps.text: Ministry of Education Regulations on Dapodik:
items: Peraturan Menteri Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan on education data management (specific regulation numbers vary; the rules are updated from time to time)
Technical guidelines (JUKNIS) for Dapodik data entry, quality standards, synchronization procedures

steps.text: Ministry of Education Regulations on Teacher Professional Development (SIMPKB):
items: Regulations on teacher certification and continuing professional development (CPD) requirements
Integration between Dapodik and SIMPKB systems

steps.text: Ministry of Finance Regulations on Record Retention:
items: Tax laws that require businesses and schools to keep financial records for 10 years (for audit purposes)
Ministry of Communication and Information Technology regulations on cybersecurity for organizations managing personal data
Requirements for incident reporting and security audits (details depend on the specific regulations in force)
Indonesian data protection law is still changing. Schools must follow regulatory updates through legal advisors, professional networks or government websites
When new regulations come out, schools should do a gap analysis and make needed changes within required timeframes (typically 6-12 months for major regulations)

content.text: Category B: Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment (Teaching & Learning)

items: Criterion B5: The school uses a variety of assessment strategies

Data protection alignment: Assessment data (EduNav gradebook, EASE results, Cambridge exam results) is managed securely and confidentially. See Section 14.3.2 (EduNav security) and Section 14.8 (Cambridge exam data security)

content.text: Category D: Resources (Facilities, Equipment, and Technology)

items: Criterion D1: The school has enough resources to support its mission
Data protection alignment: Investment in secure IT systems, data protection training and cybersecurity tools shows that the school commits resources
Criterion D2: The school maintains safe, functional, and well-maintained facilities
Data protection alignment: Physical security (locked storage, secure exam room) protects data; facilities support confidentiality (Section 14.3.1)
Criterion D3: The school provides appropriate technology and resources
Data protection alignment: Technology resources (EduNav, Dapodik, Cambridge systems) are used responsibly, with data protection safeguards (Section 14.3.2 - digital security)
Criterion D4: The school has effective systems for managing resources
Data protection alignment: Records retention schedule (Section 14.5); access control matrix (Section 14.3.3); vendor management (Section 14.3.5); audit processes (Section 14.10)

content.text: Category C: Support for Student Personal and Academic Growth

items: Category C criterion: The school has a safe, healthy, and supportive learning environment
Data protection alignment: Students' privacy is respected; safeguarding records are protected; data breaches are prevented, and are dealt with quickly if they happen
Category C criterion: The school fosters a culture of personal and social responsibility

Data protection alignment: Digital citizenship education for students (age-appropriate lessons on protecting personal information online and respecting others' privacy). Staff model responsible data handling

The "Resources" chapter includes a detailed description of the data protection program (policies, procedures, security measures, training)
